evidence_text: Immunoregulatory Microenvironment in the Elderly Skin. Previous studies have revealed that skin T cells accumulate and maintain immune responses in the elderly. However, we questioned why these functional T cells fail to recognize and eliminate malignant cells, making elderly skin more prone to developing malignant tumors. To address this question, we examined the overall skin microenvironment in aging using the Nanostring nCounter system and 10x Xenium digital spatial RNA sequencing. The digital RNA counts of CIITA and HLA-DMA, which are involved in antigen presentation, were negatively correlated with age, whereas the counts of UBE2L3 and SOCS1, molecules that play roles in immune regulation, were positively correlated with aging. The upregulation of SOCS1 was detected in the microenvironment of the skin malignant tumors. Spatial transcriptome analysis revealed that cells with high levels of SOCS1 were distributed in upper dermis and periadnexal area, and some SOCS1-positive fibroblasts were closely lined with CD163-positive macrophages. Our study showed that the skin microenvironment in the elderly may shift to an immunoregulatory condition. Furthermore, modulating certain molecules that may be involved in shared immunoregulatory mechanisms between healthy elderly skin and malignant tumors could serve as a potential strategy for preventing malignancies in elderly skin. Introduction Previous studies revealed that aging is associated with progressive decline of immune function, called immunosenescence ( Lee et al, 2022 ; Liu et al, 2023 ). In the innate immune system, phagocytic capacities of neutrophils and macrophages decrease ( Butcher et al, 2001 , 2000 ; Moss et al, 2024 ). Uptake and presentation of antigens by dendric cells and their homing to lymph nodes are impaired ( Agrawal and Gupta, 2011 ; Wong and Goldstein, 2013 ). Elevated NK cell numbers and reduced cytotoxic function were reported ( Brauning et al, 2022 ; Weiskopf et al, 2009 ). In the adaptive immune system, the number of naïve T cells and diversity of the T-cell repertoire decrease in the elderly ( Naylor et al, 2005 ). The frequency of regulatory T cells is increased in the blood of elderly individuals ( Lages et al, 2008 ). On the other hand, elevated plasma concentrations of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF have been described in elderly populations and contribute to a lifelong continuous stimulation of the immune system, resulting in a subclinical inflammatory status defined as inflammaging ( Koelman et al, 2019 ; Li et al, 2023 ; Weiskopf et al, 2009 ). Recent studies unveiled that immune cells in tissue, including resident immune cells, form distinct local immunity different from that in blood ( Farber, 2021 ). A few decades ago, it was considered that aged skin immune system was deteriorated in its adaptive capability ( Sunderkötter et al, 1997 ). However, a previous study demonstrated that T cells in human elderly skin maintain their number, effector cytokine production, repertoire diversity, and antigen responses, whereas T cells in human blood lose the repertoire diversity and effective antigen responses ( Koguchi-Yoshioka et al, 2021 ). Furthermore, CD8 resident memory T cells, which promote tumor immunity and whose infiltration in tumors is related to favorable prognosis ( Edwards et al, 2018 ), are increased in the elderly skin ( Koguchi-Yoshioka et al, 2021 ). However, although T cells in the elderly skin maintain their functionality, the incidence of skin malignant tumors such as basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) increases in line with age ( Birch-Johansen et al, 2010 ; Dodds et al, 2014 ; Holmes et al, 2007 ; Ogata et al, 2023 ). These observations raised the question of why these functional T cells in the elderly skin overlook the mutant cells that allow the development of skin cancers. Recent reports have demonstrated that the phenotype of aged macrophages is accelerated by fibroblasts ( Gather et al, 2022 ) and that even aged hair follicle stem cells can regenerate the hair follicles in the existence of young dermis ( Ge et al, 2020 ). From these studies, we hypothesized that skin immune microenvironmental alteration in the elderly skin may induce inappropriate immune responses and allow the development of malignant tumors. We aimed to investigate the aging of the skin immune microenvironment using digital mRNA expression counts and spatial RNA-sequencing techniques. Results Immunoregulatory features in the elderly skin Normalized digital mRNA count data of 770 genes (Supplementary Data S1) from the nCounter Human AutoImmune Profiling Panel were subjected to principal component analysis to reveal that the overall gene profiles of the young and the elderly skin were evenly distributed ( Figure 1 a). Figure 1 Immunoregulatory features in elderly skin. ( a ) Primary component analysis of gene expression profiles. Light blue indicates individuals aged <60 years, and dark blue represents those aged ≥60 years. n = 12. ( b ) Top 5 genes showing the strongest positive correlation with aging, on the basis of Spearman correlation coefficients ( r -values). n = 12. ( c ) Top 5 genes showing the strongest negative correlation with aging, on the basis of Spearman correlation coefficients ( r -values). n = 12. ( d ) Immunohistochemistry of the indicated proteins in representative samples from young and elderly individuals. n = 13. Among the 770 genes mentioned earlier, 17.4% of the genes (134 of 770) had an absolute Spearman correlation coefficient >0.4 (Supplementary Data S2). The top 5 genes that showed a positive Spearman correlation with age are depicted in Figure 1 b. The count of UBE2L3 , which regulates signaling pathways such as NF-κB and GSK3β/p65 ( Zhang et al, 2022 ) and whose overexpression leads to evasion of apoptosis ( Tao et al, 2020 ), and the count of XRCC6 , exerting tumor-promoting effects through β-catenin/Wnt signaling pathway ( Zhu et al, 2016 ), were positively correlated with aging ( Figure 1 b). The count of SOCS1 negatively regulates effector cytokine signaling and effective antitumor response ( Bidgood et al, 2024 ; Ilangumaran and Rottapel, 2003 ; Liau et al, 2018 ); SKP1 , S-phase kinase-associated protein, whose overexpression promotes cancer stemness, initiation, and progression ( Hussain et al, 2022 ), and TUBB , encoding a beta-tubulin protein and greatly upregulated across various cancers ( Zhu et al, 2024 ), were also positively correlated with aging ( Figure 1 b). On the other hand, the top 5 genes that showed a negative Spearman correlation with age are depicted in Figure 1 c. The count of major histocompatibility complex class II–related genes, such as CIITA , major histocompatibility complex class II transactivator, and HLA-DMA , was negatively correlated with aging ( Figure 1 c). One of the HLA class II genes, HLA-DRB3/4 , was also negatively correlated with aging, although its r-value was not ranked among the top 5 highest negative correlations ( r = −0.5965). The ATPV601 gene, involved in lysosome acidification; GSTP1 , protecting cells from oxidants and electrophilic-mediated genomic damage; and SLC3A2 , whose downregulation mediates immune evasion ( Wu et al, 2024 ), were also negatively correlated with aging ( Figure 1 c). Possibly owing to the small sample size (n = 12), none of the 770 genes we analyzed reached statistical significance after multiple testing correction using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate method (Supplementary Data S3). However, when we divided the samples into 2 age groups, the top 5 genes ranked by absolute Spearman correlation coefficient showed significantly increased or decreased expression in the older group ( Supplementary Figure S1 ). By immunohistochemistry, the density of SOCS1-positive cells was positively correlated with aging ( r = 0.6547) ( Figure 1 d), whereas that of HLA-DR was negatively correlated with aging ( r = −0.6988) ( Figure 1 d). Collectively, our normalized digital mRNA count data suggest that elderly skin microenvironment may have immunoregulatory features and lesser ability of antigen presentation. SOCS1 expression was upregulated in the microenvironment of both cSCC and BCC We next investigated whether the genes that showed a positive or negative correlation with aging in our previous Nanostring analysis were also upregulated or downregulated in the microenvironment of cSCC and BCC, whose incidence increases remarkably with age ( Green and Olsen, 2017 ; Verkouteren et al, 2017 ), using publicly available bulk RNA-sequencing data. Among the differentially expressed genes with adjusted P < .05 and log 2 fold change > 0.5 in cSCC ( GSE139505 ) ( Das Mahapatra et al, 2020 ) or BCC ( GSE125285 ) ( Wan et al, 2021 ) compared with healthy controls, the genes positively or negatively correlated with aging in our digital count analysis were highlighted in red ( r > 0.4) or blue ( r < −0.4), respectively ( Figure 2 a and b). We performed a hypergeometric test to examine whether the genes with an absolute correlation coefficient | r | > 0.4 in our digital count analysis significantly overlapped with the genes from bulk RNA sequencing of cSCC and BCC that met the criteria of adjusted P < .05 and log 2 fold change > 0.5. Using the 758 genes shared between the bulk RNA-sequencing and our NanoString platforms, the results showed P = .99 for cSCC and P = .77 for BCC, indicating no statistically significant overlap between age-correlated genes in our digital count analysis and the significantly altered genes in cSCC or BCC. However, among these highlighted genes ( Figure 2 a and b), the expression of SOCS1 , which was positively correlated with aging in our Nanostring data ( r = 0.6547), was upregulated in both cSCC and BCC (cSCC: log 2 fold change = 1.51, P = 1.36E-08; BCC: log 2 fold change = 1.34, P = 1.25E-13). Figure 2 SOCS1 expression was upregulated in the microenvironment of both cSCC and BCC. ( a ) DEGs in cSCC compared with those in healthy controls, based on GSE139505 . ( b ) DEGs in BCC compared with those in healthy controls, based on GSE125285 . The x-axis represents log 2 FC, and the y-axis represents −log 10 of the adjusted P -value. Among the DEGs with adjusted P < .05 and log 2 FC > 0.5, genes that are positively or negatively correlated with aging (red: r > 0.4, blue: r < −0.4) in the digital count analysis shown in Figure 1 are highlighted. BCC, basal cell carcinoma; DEG, differentially expressed gene; FC, fold change; cSCC, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. The 10x Xenium enables visualization of SOCS1-producing cells, their localization, and interacting cells Because SOCS1 plays a critical role in limiting effector cytokine signaling and effective antitumor response ( Bidgood et al, 2024 ) and because its expression was positively correlated with age and upregulated in skin malignancies, we focused on the sources of SOCS1 as a potential molecule that may protect aged skin from malignant tumors. The spatial transcriptome analysis using 10x Xenium using upper-arm skin specimens from 3 donors with different ages depicted that SOCS1 -positive cells were distributed in the upper dermis and periadnexal area in all ages ( Figure 3 a). The differentially expressed gene analysis revealed that the sources of SOCS1 were fibroblasts, T cells, macrophages, sebocytes, and sweat gland cells, suggesting that SOCS1 -positive cells are not restricted to a single cell type (Supplementary Data S4 and S5). We compared the normalized counts of cells classified as fibroblasts and CD8 T cells, which were identified as the source of SOCS1 in all samples (Supplementary Data S5), and found no significant age-related differences in expression among the 3 samples ( Supplementary Figure S2 ) (fibroblasts: P = .2217; CD8 T cells: P = .1620). However, on the basis of the clustering data, we found that the populations with the highest total counts, clusters 1 and 2, in all samples were identified as fibroblasts (Supplementary Data S5). Thus, we next assessed the distribution of SOCS1-expressing fibroblasts, which were one of the most abundantly observed SOCS1 -expressing cell types. These SOCS1 -expressing fibroblasts either exist solely ( Figure 3 b), connect with other fibroblasts ( Figure 3 c), or interact with immune cells in the stroma in the skin. Some of these fibroblasts were adjacent to CD163 -positive macrophages ( Figure 3 d), whereas CD163-positive macrophages were also found next to other cell types, such as endothelial cells ( Figure 3 e). Discussion We aimed to investigate the immune microenvironment of aging skin and found that major histocompatibility complex class II–related genes were negatively correlated with age, whereas immunoregulatory genes were positively correlated. This may suggest that elderly skin microenvironment loses effective immune responses and the ability of antigen presentation, implying that elderly skin microenvironment can be the environment where the tumor cells can be overlooked by immune cells. By applying spatial transcriptome analysis, we could investigate in detail not only the transcripts retained by each cell type but also the proximity and potential interactions among various cell types. Our spatial transcriptome analysis revealed that SOCS1 , which was positively correlated with aging in our analyses, is expressed not only by immune cells but also by stromal cells such as fibroblasts. This highlights the importance of considering the microenvironment, including stromal cells, when analyzing immune cells residing in tissues. Possible explanations for the positive correlation between SOCS1 expression and aged skin include previously reported factors, including chronic infections such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Carow et al, 2011 ), hepatitis C virus ( Zhang et al, 2011 ), and cytomegalovirus ( Shin et al, 2015 ) as well as oxidative stress ( Kim et al, 2020 ) and accumulated epigenetic alterations ( Cheng et al, 2014 ). Although the present Nanostring analysis was conducted using trunk skin samples, it is also plausible that cumulative exposure to UVR may contribute to this association ( Friedrich et al, 2003 ). SOCS1 -expressing fibroblasts, which constitute a major cell type expressing SOCS1 , were found either as isolated cells within the stroma or adjacent to stromal cells or immune cells, such as CD163 -positive macrophages, a marker of tumor-associated macrophages ( Mathiesen et al, 2025 ) and immunomodulatory M2 macrophages ( Chen et al, 2023 ). The effects of SOCS1 vary depending on the cell type. Even within the same cell context, there are contrasting reports, ranging from studies demonstrating impaired antitumor immunity due to reduced cytokine production to those showing immunostimulatory and antitumor effects. In T cells, high expression of SOCS1 in T cells from patients correlates with low acute graft-versus-host disease occurrence after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, suggesting that SOCS1 suppresses T-cell activation ( Guo et al, 2022 ). Moreover, in a mouse model, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated inactivation of SOCS1 in tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes enhanced responsiveness to cytokine signaling and increased antitumor activity in vivo ( Schlabach et al, 2023 ). In macrophages, TNF production was increased in SOCS1-knockout mice ( Kinjyo et al, 2002 ), and silencing SOCS1 promoted polarization toward a proinflammatory M1 phenotype ( Liang et al, 2017 ). Overall, SOCS1 plays an immunoregulatory role in immune cells. In fibroblasts, SOCS1 inhibited cell growth and induced cellular senescence ( Calabrese et al, 2009 ). Another study showed that overexpression of SOCS1 suppressed collagen production ( Shoda et al, 2007 ). In a chondrocytic cell line, overexpression of SOCS1 suppressed signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 pathway while enhancing the MAPK pathway ( Ben-Zvi et al, 2006 ). In the tumor biology, repressed SOCS1 gene by epigenetic alteration such as promoter CpG methylation or microRNA has been reported in various cancers, including hepatocellular carcinoma ( Yoshikawa et al, 2001 ), multiple myeloma ( Galm et al, 2003 ), prostate cancer ( Kobayashi et al, 2012 ), and breast cancer ( Jiang et al, 2010 ), among others, indicating the antitumor effects of SOCS1. Conversely, in melanoma cells, repression of SOCS1 has been shown to inhibit proliferation and induce apoptosis ( Yu and Long, 2017 ), highlighting the dichotomous roles of SOCS1 in tumor, which may be context dependent on the basis of the organ and its microenvironment. Further studies are needed to elucidate the cell type–, organ-, and microenvironment-specific functions of SOCS1. Our study revealed that SOCS1 was positively correlated with aging and upregulated in common skin malignancies such as cSCC and BCC. Given that SOCS1 expression is elevated in aged skin and considering reports that SOCS1 inactivation enhances tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy ( Schlabach et al, 2023 ) and that SOCS1-silenced dendritic cells improve the efficacy of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy ( Zheng et al, 2021 ) in mouse models, a comprehensive evaluation of cell-specific SOCS1 function in both the normal skin and tumor microenvironments may lead to a new strategy targeting SOCS1-expressing stromal cells to prevent tumor development in elderly skin. Limitations of this study include the relatively small number of digital mRNA counts and spatial transcriptome analyses performed. In addition, the number of panel genes, particularly in the spatial transcriptome, was limited. Although the primary aim of this study was to investigate the skin microenvironment in aged individuals, further studies are warranted to validate our findings through in vitro experiments using human fibroblasts, which examine the role of SOCS1 and its interactions with immune cells, such as macrophages, as well as with skin cancer cells. Further accumulation of human sample data would overcome these limitations. In conclusion, our study demonstrated that the microenvironment of elderly skin shifts toward an immunoregulatory states. The SOCS1 , which is positively correlated with aging skin and upregulated in skin malignant tumors, is expressed by both immune cells and stromal cells, some of which are found in contact with regulatory immune cells. Modulating the functions and interactions of these molecules, which may be involved in a common immunoregulatory mechanism in both healthy elderly skin and malignant tumors, could potentially help to protect elderly skin from tumor development. Materials and Methods Human subjects All study protocols were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and were approved by the Ethics Committee of Osaka University Hospital (number 20158). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The list of samples obtained is provided in Supplementary Table S1 . The specimens used for digital mRNA counting and immunohistochemical staining were obtained from individuals who visited our hospital between 2019 and 2023, whereas the specimens for the 10x Xenium analysis were obtained from individuals who visited between 2023 and 2024. The 10x Xenium (HC1–3) and Nanostring (sample number 1–12) data were obtained from 4-mm punch biopsies of healthy individuals with no evidence of skin or systemic disease. The immunohistochemical samples (sample numbers 13–25) were obtained from individuals without systemic disease and include surplus skin grafts collected during treatment for benign skin tumors that required grafting. These grafts were obtained from sites at least 30 cm away from the skin benign tumor and were confirmed by at least 1 board-certified dermatologist to be free of any skin lesions. Preparation of mRNA and digital mRNA count Total RNA was isolated from frozen 12 healthy human skin samples from the trunk (ages: 42–94 years) using E.Z.N.A. Total RNA Kit I (Omega Biotek), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA concentrations were quantified, and the OD260/230 and the OD260/280 ratios were confirmed to be >1.6 and 1.8, respectively. Gene expression was quantified by NanoString nCounter system (NanoString Technologies) with nCounter Human AutoImmune Profiling Panel. Data analysis was conducted using nSolver 4.0. Normalized RNA counts data are provided in Supplementary Data S1. Heatmap was generated using iDEP1.1 ( http://bioinformatics.sdstate.edu/idep11/ ) and provided in Supplementary Data S2. Immunohistochemical staining Immunohistochemical staining for HLA-DR and SOCS1 was performed on serial paraffin-embedded sections of 13 normal skin samples (ages 14–86 years). The list of samples is provided in Supplementary Table S1 . After standard deparaffinization, antigen retrieval was carried out as follows: for anti-SOCS1, heating in a 120 °C oil bath for 11 minutes with citrate buffer (pH 6.0), followed by incubation for 30 minutes at room temperature; for anti-HLA-DR, heating in an oil bath for 16 minutes with EDTA buffer (pH 9.0), followed by incubation for 30 minutes at room temperature. The sections were subsequently washed with Tween-PBS. To prevent nonspecific signals, sections were blocked with Blocking One Histo (Nacalai Tesque) for 30 minutes. Primary antibodies were then applied at room temperature for 30 minutes: a monoclonal rabbit antibody against HLA-DR (number ab92511; Abcam, dilution 1:10000) and a polyclonal rabbit antibody against SOCS1 (number ab137384; Abcam, dilution 1:100). Secondary staining was performed using the Dako REAL Detection System (Dako, Carpinteria, CA). Reactions were visualized using the ABC developing system (Vector Laboratories), and sections were counterstained with hematoxylin (Vector Laboratories). All immunohistochemically stained sections were imaged using a Keyence BZ-X710 microscope (Keyence). The quantification using high-power fields was performed by a single individual who was blinded to the age of the participants. Five random high-power fields (×400 magnification) were selected, and the number of positive cells was counted in each field to calculate the average. Identification of differentially expressed genes in cSCC and BCC We analyzed differentially expressed genes in cSCC and BCC using publicly available RNA-sequencing datasets from the National Center for Biotechnology Information ( GSE139505 and GSE125285 ). The GSE139505 dataset includes 7 control samples and 9 cSCC cases ( Das Mahapatra et al, 2020 ) ( Supplementary Table S1 ), whereas the GSE125285 dataset comprises 25 control samples and 25 BCC cases ( Wan et al, 2021 ) ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Differential expression analysis was performed using the RaNAseq pipeline ( https://ranaseq.eu/home ). Raw FASTQ files were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38). Gene-level counts were obtained with featureCounts, and differential expression analysis was conducted using DESeq2, in which multiple testing correction of P -values in differential expression analysis is performed by default using the Benjamini–Hochberg method to control the false discovery rate ( Love et al, 2014 ). Genes with a P < .05 were considered differentially expressed. Volcano plots were generated using GraphPad Prism, version 9.3.1 (GraphPad Software). The 10x Xenium in situ In situ gene expression profiling was performed using the Xenium platform (10x Genomics), following the protocols provided by the manufacturer. Tissue sections, 5 μm in thickness, were prepared from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks according to the “Xenium In Situ for FFPE-Tissue Preparation Guide” ( CG000578 Rev C, 10x Genomics). These sections were carefully mounted onto the sample area of a Xenium slide (PN-1000465), followed by deparaffinization and permeabilization as detailed in the Xenium Fixation and Permeabilization Protocol ( CG000580 Rev C, 10x Genomics). The probe hybridization mix was prepared using the 10x Genomics Xenium Human Skin Gene Expression Panel (260 genes) with an additional customized panel (Xenium Custom Gene Expression Panel, design identification: P3HCWE) (Supplementary Data S6). The custom panel was designed using the Xenium Panel Designer following the Xenium Add-on Panel Design Technical Note ( CG000643 Rev B, 10x Genomics). During the Xenium Analyzer workflow, the Xenium In Situ Cell Segmentation reagents (PN-100661) were used to automate cell boundary identification with a multitissue stain mix. This mix included antibodies for membrane labeling, antibodies for intracellular labeling, a universal ribosomal RNA label, and DAPI for nuclear staining. Probe hybridization, ligation, amplification, cell segmentation staining, and autofluorescence quenching were carried out according to the Xenium In Situ Gene Expression with Cell Segmentation Staining User Guide ( CG000749 Rev A, 10x Genomics). The slides were then processed with the Xenium Analyzer for imaging and analysis, following the Decoding and Imaging User Guide ( CG000584 Rev E, 10x Genomics). The instrument software (version 3.0.2.0) and analysis software (version 3.0.0.15) were used. Output images and gene expression profiles were evaluated using Xenium Explorer, version 3.1.0. After the Xenium analysis, H&E staining was applied to the Xenium slide. For quality control, the output summary HTML file generated by the Xenium Analyzer was reviewed, and no errors were reported. Cell clustering was performed using the default pipeline implemented in the 10x Genomics Xenium platform. Briefly, raw transcript counts were aggregated for each segmented cell to generate a cell-by-gene expression matrix. The expression values were normalized and log transformed to minimize the influence of highly expressed genes and to stabilize variance across cells. Dimensionality reduction was then conducted using principal component analysis, followed by graph-based clustering. A k-nearest neighbor graph was constructed in the reduced principal component analysis space on the basis of transcriptomic similarity between cells. Clusters were identified using the Louvain community detection algorithm, which partitions the graph into groups of cells with high internal connectivity. For visualization, clustered cells were projected onto a 2-dimensional Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection embedding, and cluster identities were also mapped back onto the tissue section using spatial coordinates derived from cell segmentation. Each cluster was automatically assigned a unique color in the Xenium Explorer interface. Clusters were annotated manually on the basis of the following marker gene expression and histological location of the skin: LUM , COL5A2 , COL6A2 , and COL6A3 for fibroblast; keratin 5 gene K5 and TP63 for stratum basale; CLDN1 and keratin gene 2 gene K2 for stratum granulosum; KRTDAP for stratum spinosum; ACTA2 , CALD1 , and TAGLN for myofibroblasts; MLANA and PMEL for melanocytes; CD1A for Langerhans cell; VWF and CDH5 for vascular endothelial cell; PROX1 for LYVE1 for lymphatic endothelial cell; TAGLN and NR2F2 for vascular smooth muscle cell; CD3D , CD3E , CD3G , and CD4 for CD4 T cell; CD3D , CD3E , CD3G , and CD8A for CD8 T cell; FOXP3 , CD3D , CD3E , and CD3G for regulatory T cell; CD68 for macrophage; CD68 and CD163 for CD163-positive macrophage; RHEB and FABP5 for sebocytes; keratin 5 gene K5 and INSIG1 for sebaceous gland-peripheral layer; keratin 15 gene K15 , CXADR , and CRABP2 for sweat duct cell; keratin 15 gene K15 and MARCKSL1 for sweat gland secretory cell; FABP4 and ENPP1 for adipocyte; S100B , CDH19 , and EDNRB for neural cell. Spatial transcriptomic data were processed and visualized using 10x Genomics Xenium Explorer (version 3.1.0). Individual transcript molecules were detected through multiplexed in situ hybridization and decoded through sequential imaging and barcode readout. Each transcript was assigned to a specific gene target and mapped to its corresponding (x, y) spatial coordinates within the tissue section. For visualization, detected transcripts were rendered as individual spots (dots) overlaid on the tissue image and/or segmented cell boundaries. Transcripts were displayed at single-molecule resolution. Gene-specific expression could be viewed by selecting target genes within the Explorer interface, and transcript spots corresponding to the selected genes were shown in designated colors. Normalization of the data shown in Supplementary Figure S2 was performed using Seurat’s NormalizeData function with the parameter normalization.method set to 'LogNormalize.' Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test was performed using GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software). Statistics Statistical analyses for Figure 1 b–d were performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad Software). The Spearman rank correlation coefficients were calculated using the same software. For Figure 1 b and c, the adjusted P -values were calculated using the Benjamini–Hochberg method for multiple testing correction, and the results are provided in Supplementary Data S3. In addition, the same dataset shown in Figure 1 a–c was reanalyzed by dividing the samples into 2 groups using age 60 years as a cutoff, and the results are presented in Supplementary Figure S1 . This analysis was performed using the Mann–Whitney test in Prism 10 (GraphPad Software). The analysis methods for the public bulk RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 2 and the 10x Xenium spatial transcriptomics data shown in Figure 3 are described in detail earlier. evidence_text:
Single-cell spatial analysis identifies ID1-high endothelial cells in tertiary lymphoid structures as predictors of durable response to immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer. BACKGROUND: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) maturity and cellular composition shape resistance or sensitivity to immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) across cancers. Single-cell spatial resolution data for the endothelial compartment of TLSs are lacking; therefore, we investigated the cellular composition, endothelial dynamics, and cell-cell interactions within TLS regions. METHODS: We applied high-resolution Xenium In Situ spatial transcriptomics to eight samples collected from non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLC) (four after chemoimmunotherapy, four untreated), extracted 90 TLS regions, generated approximately 320,000 single-cell profiles from those regions, and analyzed the endothelial compartment within each TLS. We independently assessed the exploratory findings using multiplex immunofluorescence and survival analysis in a separate cohort of 45 patients receiving immunotherapy. RESULTS: Spatial mapping revealed a reproducible, B-cell-dominant TLS architecture across all samples. Mature TLSs contained CXCL13-rich follicular cores and were associated with a favorable prognosis. Within the endothelial compartment, high endothelial cells (HECs) forming high-endothelial venules (HEVs) segregated from other endothelial cells; in mature TLSs these HECs exhibited high inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1) expression and an adhesion molecular signature, promoting lymphocyte recruitment. Patients with tumors harboring ID1-high HEVs showed higher response rates and pronounced survival advantage; multivariable analysis confirmed ID1-high status as an independent prognostic factor. Conversely, ICB exposure eventually reduced ID1 expression and adhesion molecule levels in HECs, impaired lymphocyte trafficking, and promoted a shift toward a remodeled endothelial state. CONCLUSIONS: ID1expression, linked to HEC differentiation during TLS maturation or ICB exposure, marks a functionally mature, lymphocyte-recruiting HEV that predict durable response to immunotherapy. These findings provide a novel mechanistic framework and practical biomarkers for HEV-centered immuno-oncology strategies in NSCLC. Keywords:  Biomarker, CXCL12, High endothelial venules, ID1, Immunotherapy, Non-small-cell lung cancer, Remodeling, Spatial single-cell analysis, Spatial transcriptomics, Tertiary lymphoid structures      status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Received 2025 Aug 21; Accepted 2025 Dec 27; Collection date 2026.       Introduction  Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide [ 1 ]. Platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy combining cytotoxic agents with immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) has extended survival in some patients and is standard both as a neoadjuvant setting and a first-line treatment for advanced disease [ 2 – 5 ]. Despite ongoing real-world data analyses, reliable biomarkers capable of definitively distinguishing durable responders from non-responders are needed [ 6 ,  7 ].  The presence and maturity of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) within the tumor microenvironment have emerged as key prognostic and predictive elements across multiple solid tumors [ 8 – 10 ]. In NSCLC, the densities of DC-LAMP⁺ mature dendritic cells and CD20⁺ B cells within TLSs are correlated with long-term survival [ 11 ,  12 ]. Mature TLSs are linked to favorable ICI response in various types of cancers, such as NSCLC and bladder cancer, and then high levels of intra-tumoral CXCL13 expression mark patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer likely to respond to treatment [ 13 ,  14 ].  The canonical 12-chemokine “TLS gene signature” is employed to predict TLS regions in transcriptomic analyses [ 15 ,  16 ]. However, its expression varies across tumor types, underscoring the inter-cancer TLS heterogeneity and the need for more tumor-specific functional TLS markers [ 17 ]. Our re-analysis of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to isolate TLS-like cells with the 12-chemokine scores yielded few B-cell populations in breast ( n  = 26) and lung ( n  = 185) cancer samples (Supplementary Fig. S1A, B) [ 18 ,  19 ], highlighting the limitations of dissociative single-cell methods for analyzing structured niches. Therefore, spatially resolved transcriptomics is essential for capturing TLS architecture and heterogeneity in situ.  Previous studies have investigated spatial transcriptomics focused on TLS [ 20 – 22 ]. Immature TLSs enriched with immunosuppressive macrophages and regulatory T cells confer resistance to ICB, particularly in peritoneal metastases in gastric cancer [ 23 ]. Additionally, tumors containing mature TLSs can exhibit primary ICB resistance driven by distinct cancer-associated fibroblast subsets (FAP⁺ αSMA⁺ and MYH11⁺ αSMA⁺) in NSCLC [ 24 ]. Collectively, these studies demonstrated the effects of both TLS maturity and cellular composition on therapeutic outcomes. However, to date, the spatiotemporal dynamics of endothelial cells within TLSs have not been assessed using single-cell resolution methods.  Therefore, the present study applied high-resolution Xenium In Situ spatial single-cell transcriptomics to resected NSCLC specimens. We investigated the cellular components, endothelial cell dynamics, and cell–cell interactions within TLS associated region by TLS maturity and treatment status with or without chemo-immunotherapy. The study design is shown in Fig.  1 . The resulting dataset provides a foundational atlas of TLS regions in NSCLC and highlights inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1)-high endothelial venules (HEVs) as a potential biomarker, offering insights to guide new immunotherapeutic approaches or enhance the effectiveness of current treatments.    Fig. 1   Study design and cohorts. ( A ) Xenium discovery cohort: profiling of eight resected NSCLC specimens (four neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, four untreated) using spatial single-cell transcriptomics allowed the manual annotation of 90 TLS regions for downstream analyses. ( B ) Biomarker validation cohort: 45 archival NSCLC resections from patients treated with immune-checkpoint blockade after recurrence were interrogated by multiplex immunofluorescence for TLS/HEV markers and linked to overall patient survival                     Materials and methods   Patients and samples  Tissue specimens and clinical records from patients with NSCLC were collected at 14 Japanese institutions between January 2017 and February 2024. Consistent with the KEYNOTE-189, CheckMate-816, and CheckMate-9LA protocols [ 2 ,  4 ,  5 ], patients harboring major EGFR mutations or ALK rearrangements were excluded.  In the xenium discovery cohort, we initially identified 29 patients who underwent surgical resection within the preceding two years, with or without neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy. Patients who achieved clinical complete response after the neoadjuvant therapy or received perioperative radiotherapy were excluded. Furthermore, we selected eight patients showing TLSs enrichment in immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis (as described below) and with an RNA DV200 ≥ 30%. Given the limited tissue from pre-treatment bronchoscopic biopsies, matched pre-/post-treatment pairs were not available, and independent resected specimens were used for Xenium analysis. Therefore, the final analysis included four patients who received neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy and four patients who underwent surgery without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, analyzed as independent patient samples (Supplementary Fig. S2A, B). In the biomarker validation cohort using multiplex-immunofluorescence (MIF), 683 patients who underwent ICB with or without chemotherapy were initially screened. Among these, 575 patients were excluded because the available specimens were derived from bronchoscopy, metastatic-site biopsy, computed tomography-guided needle biopsy, or because no residual tissue remained. Archived lung specimens obtained prior to any immunotherapy exposure were available from 108 surgical cases. Among these, 45 patients who later initiated immunotherapy within two years after postoperative recurrence were enrolled for MIF (as described below), and survival analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3).  Additionally, we retrieved a scRNA-seq dataset comprising 26 breast cancer specimens from the GEO (accession  GSE176078 ) and downloaded an integrated scRNA-seq dataset of 185 NSCLC specimens from Figshare (DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.6222221.v3).    Treatment responses and survival evaluation  Clinical variables, including age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, smoking history, histology, programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score (PD-L1 TPS), clinical stage, and treatment outcomes, were extracted from patient records. PD-L1 TPS was measured with the 22C3 antibody. Radiographic responses were categorized according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1 [ 25 ]. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from chemo-immunotherapy initiation to death or the last follow-up. The data cut-off date was March 31, 2025.    IHC and MIF examination  Chromogenic IHC was performed on 5 μm formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) lung-cancer sections after Tris-EDTA retrieval (pH 9.0, 95 °C, 40 min) and peroxidase quenching (Dako REAL). Serial sections were incubated at 4 °C overnight with primary antibodies including anti-CD3 (Proteintech, #60181-1-Ig, 1:800), anti-CD20 (Proteintech, #60271-1-Ig, 1:1000), and anti-PNAd (BioLegend, clone MECA-79, #120801, 1:100). Detection was performed using an HRP–DAB system following the manufacturers’ instructions. MIF was performed with two four-marker panels. Panel 1: CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), CD23-CL594 (Proteintech, clone 4C7C9, #CL594-60208-2, 1:100), CD3-CL647 (Proteintech, clone 3F3A1, #CL647-60181, 1:100), and CXCL12 (CST, clone D8G6H, #97958, 1:100); Panel 2: MECA-79-AF488 (Invitrogen, clone MECA-79, #53-6-36–82, 1:50), CD31 (Proteintech, clone 3F8E2, #66065-2-Ig, 1:100), CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), and ID1 (CST, clone F2M1J, #23369, 1:100).  Fluorescence was detected using the following secondary antibodies: donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 488, donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 647, donkey anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, 1:500, 1 h, room temperature), and goat anti-rabbit CoraLite Plus 750 (Proteintech, 1:200, 1 h, RT). The slides were mounted in antifade medium with DAPI (Invitrogen) and imaged on an FV3000 confocal microscope (Olympus) with 20×, 40×, and 60× objectives under identical laser and gain settings.    IHC quantification  TLSs were identified with a two-step procedure as previously described [ 26 ]. First, serial sections were immunostained for CD20 (B cells), CD3 (T cells), and PNAd (HEV). TLS-positive specimens showed clusters of T cells surrounding aggregates of B cells. Second, TLSs were divided into three status by B-cell density and follicular architecture: absent, immature, and mature. CXCL12 protein level was quantified using ImageJ (v 2.9.0/1.53t) as the mean percentage of the TLS area with positive staining in three representative fields. Cases above and below the cohort median (excluding TLS-negative samples) were classified as CXCL12-high and CXCL12-low, respectively. ID1 status was determined by counting ID1-positive endothelial cells in HEVs within TLSs across three representative microscopic fields. Specimens with a mean count ≥ 10 and < 10 cells were classified as ID1-high and ID1-low, respectively. Two investigators trained in digital histopathology reviewed the images independently and were blinded to the clinical data. Discrepancies were resolved by joint review, and the final status was verified by an additional pathologist.    Xenium in situ workflow  Five-micron FFPE sections (DV200 ≥ 30%) containing TLSs by IHC were processed using the Xenium FFPE workflow (see 10x Genomics,  CG000601  Rev B). After de-paraffinization, decrosslinking, and Tris-EDTA retrieval, the slides were hybridized overnight at 50 °C with a 430-gene probe set (10 nM each, 380-gene Human Immune-Oncology base panel plus 50 custom endothelial-focused custom genes; Supplementary Table S1), then ligated and amplified by rolling-circle amplification. The prepared slides were run on the Xenium Analyzer, which executed 15 automated cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and stripping, capturing 0.75 μm Z-stacks across the entire 12 × 24 mm imaging area. The on-instrument pipeline stitched fields of view, segmented nuclei/cells from DAPI, and decoded transcripts by maximum-likelihood matching to the gene codebook. Transcripts with calibrated Q-scores ≥ 20 were retained. A cell-by-gene count matrix, segmentation masks; and morphology images were exported for downstream analysis.    Xenium in situ analyses  Cell segmentation morphology images generated by the Xenium Analyzer were co-registered with the corresponding H&E images, after which every TLS was manually delineated, and the constituent cells were extracted for downstream analysis (Supplementary Fig. S4). TLS boundaries were drawn to encompass contiguous clusters of immune cells. All spatial transcriptomic analyses in this study were restricted to cells located within these manually annotated TLS regions of interest. Tumor parenchyma outside the TLS boundaries was not included in the expression matrices used for any downstream analyses.  All analyses were carried out using R software (v 4.4.2) and Python (v 3.12.9). Using Seurat package (v 5.2.1), we generated a separate Seurat object for each TLS and removed low-quality cells (< 5 detected genes and < 10 total transcript counts). All TLS objects were then pooled into a single Seurat object for downstream processing. Gene expression matrices were normalized using the NormalizeData function, variable features were identified with the FindVariableFeatures function, and linear scaling was applied using the ScaleData function. PCA was performed with the RunPCA function and the optimal number of principal components (PCs) was selected from the ElbowPlot. Batch effects arising from sample identity were corrected by applying the RunHarmony function to the PCA embeddings, and clustering was conducted on the Harmony-integrated PCs using the Louvain algorithm [ 27 ]. The same embeddings were used to generate Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualizations.  Because spatial transcriptomics can misassign transcripts to neighboring cells, the cell-type annotation did not rely solely on canonical markers. Rather, candidate markers for each cluster were identified using FindMarkers function (log fold-change > 0.20;  P  < 0.01), and the resulting labels were imported into Xenium Explorer, where they were cross-validated against cellular morphology and histological context (e.g., endothelial cells continuity). Higher-resolution analyses were performed for endothelial cells, with each population re-extracted into a new Seurat object, dimensional reduction and clustering repeated as described above, and cell-type identities refined (Supplementary Table S2) [ 15 ,  28 – 31 ]. Mixed clusters were similarly reclassified, and the final cell-type labels were appended to the metadata of the main object.  Differentially expressed genes were identified for each cell type with two-sided t-tests, with significance thresholds of |log₂ fold change| ≥ 0.20 and  P  < 0.01. Genes that met these criteria were subjected to Gene Ontology overrepresentation analysis to elucidate the biological pathways that were preferentially affected in each comparison. Cell–cell communications (CCIs) were reconstructed using CellChat package (v 2.1.2), which quantitatively infers ligand–receptor interaction networks from scRNA-seq profiles. To place these interactions in their spatial context, we subsequently analyzed the CCIs within each field of view, including TLSs, using stLearn (v 0.4.10).    Statistical analyses  Continuous variables and dichotomous variables are summarized as medians with inter-quartile ranges and absolute counts with percentages, respectively. Group differences in categorical data were assessed with Pearson’s χ² or Fisher’s exact tests, as appropriate. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare TLS counts and the cellular compositions stratified by TLS maturity and treatment arm. OS was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier curves (log-rank test) and modelled using Cox proportional-hazards regression. The independent correlates of TLS maturation and CXCL12/ID1 status were identified with multivariable logistic regression. All analyses were performed in R (v 4.4.2), and two-sided P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.     Results   Spatial single-cell atlas reveals B-cell-dominated TLS architecture independent of neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy  The eight-patient Xenium discovery cohort is summarized in Table  1 . Apart from a slightly younger median age in the ICB plus chemotherapy arm, the two groups were well balanced for sex, clinical stage, histological subtype and PD-L1 TPS. Neoadjuvant treatment produced one pathological complete response, with partial responses in the remaining cases. A density map from Xenium Explorer demonstrated that a composite oncogenic signature, based on  CEACAM6 ,  EGFR ,  EPCAM ,  ERBB2 ,  ERBB3 ,  MET ,  MUC5AC  and  TMPRSS2 , closely tracked with therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, serial sections confirmed PNAd-positive HEV in all TLSs (Supplementary Fig. S5). After filtering, 319,909 cells were retained and classified based on canonical markers into 16 cell-type clusters: conventional B cells (Bconv), follicular B cells (FoB), proliferating B cells, conventional CD4⁺ T cells (CD4_Tconv), follicular-helper T cells (Tfh), regulatory T cells (Treg), CD8⁺ T cells, plasma cells, macrophages, mature and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (mDC, pDC), mast cells, neutrophils, endothelial cells, fibroblasts and tumor cells (Fig.  2 A). Unintegrated UMAPs showed specimen-specific clustering; however, harmony correction merged cells from all eight samples into shared lineage islands, indicating effective removal of batch effects (Fig.  2 B). Overlaying these annotations on matched H&E images reproduced the classical TLS blueprint: FoB and proliferating B cells packed the germinal-center core; CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells formed concentric mantles; and plasma, DCs and endothelial cells ringed the periphery (Fig.  2 D) [ 33 ].  The cellular composition was strikingly reproducible across patients. B-cell subsets dominated, with Bconv (18.5%) and FoB (17.6%) together comprising ~ 36%, and proliferating B cells adding 2.8%. T-cell populations accounted for ~ 33%: CD4_Tconv 17.7%, CD8⁺ T 11.4%, Tfh 2.2% and Treg 1.6%. Overall, spatial single-cell mapping yielded a reproducible B-cell-centered TLS atlas that was consistent across all samples.    TLS maturation reshapes immune niches and improves survival under cancer immunotherapy  To minimize therapy-related bias, TLS maturation was interrogated exclusively in untreated controls. Representative Xenium Explorer and MIF findings readily distinguished compact, mantle-ringed B-cell follicles from loosely organized, T-cell–rich aggregates, designating the former as mature and the latter as immature.  CXCL13 ,  CXCR5 ,  FCER2  and  MS4A1  were highly concentrated in mature cores; their combined expression was converted into a “mature-TLS score” with AddModuleScore function (Fig.  3 A) [ 34 ,  35 ]. Using a threshold of 0 separated 22 mature (≥ 0) and 26 immature (< 0) structures (Fig.  3 B), and visual overlays of TLS maturation showed near-perfect concordance with histology (Fig.  3 C). Area-normalized transcriptional profiling of the 13 chemokines and their receptors revealed a sharp dichotomy (Fig.  3 D): mature TLSs contained significantly more  CXCL13  and  CXCR4 , whereas immature TLSs were enriched for  CCL2 ,  CCL3 ,  CCL4 ,  CCL5 ,  CCL8 ,  CCL18  and the IFN-inducible  CXCL9–11  cluster. TLS-area–adjusted cell counts mirrored these findings, with higher densities of every B-cell subset in mature TLSs, and predominantly CD8⁺ T cells, macrophages, mDCs and endothelial cells in their immature counterparts (Fig.  3 E). In mature TLSs, fibroblasts showed higher  CXCL12 , whereas FoBs exhibited elevated  CXCR4  [ 36 ]. Tfh cells expressed abundant  CXCL13  together with  CXCR5  on B cells [ 33 ]. In contrast, immature TLSs exhibited a Th1-skewed inflammatory milieu characterized by  CXCL9  from IFN-γ-responsive macrophages and DCs, and higher  IFIT3  in CD8⁺ T cells. Endothelial transcriptomics reinforced this functional divergence: mature TLS vasculature preferentially expressed PNAd-associated genes, such as  CHST4  and  B3GNT3  together with adhesion molecules, including  SELP  and  ICAM1 , whereas immature TLSs overexpressed the HEV-developmental receptors  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14  (Fig.  3 F and Supplementary Fig. S6). Gene Ontology analysis echoed these contrasts, identifying enrichment of adaptive B-cell programs in mature TLSs and pathways governing lymphocyte migration, cell–cell adhesion, and activation thresholds in immature TLSs (Fig.  3 G).  Kaplan–Meier curves in immunotherapy-treated patients demonstrated that mature TLSs conferred a substantial survival advantage over immature or absent TLSs (median OS 60.2 vs. 21.4 months; log-rank  P  = 0.037) (Fig.  3 H). Collectively, these spatial and transcriptional features characterize TLS maturation states and demonstrate their prognostic relevance in patients receiving immunotherapy.    ID1-high HEVs in mature TLS are associated with better survival in patients receiving immunotherapy  Unsupervised UMAP analysis of the pre-processed, normalized endothelial subset resolved two transcriptionally discrete vascular clusters: high endothelial cell (HEC) and blood endothelial cell (BEC) (Fig.  4 A and Supplementary Fig. S7). The HEC cluster was characterized by robust expression of classical HEV genes, including  ACKR1 ,  SELP ,  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14 , confirming its HEV-like phenotype (Fig.  4 B) [ 30 ]. MIF of resected samples corroborated the spatial coexistence of both HEC- and BEC-type vessels within mature TLSs in situ (Fig.  4 C). Differential-expression analysis of HECs revealed significant upregulation of  ID1  in mature TLSs compared with immature TLSs (Fig.  4 D,  P  < 0.05). Compared with the other ID family members,  ID2  and  ID4 ,  ID1  was selectively expressed in endothelial cells, with the highest levels observed in HECs (Fig.  4 E, F). We further re-analyzed an integrated scRNA-seq dataset comprising 185 NSCLC samples to validate ID-family expression in the vascular compartment [ 19 ].  ID1  expression was largely confined to malignant epithelial and endothelial cells. Within the endothelial lineage, its expression was observed across several subpopulations, including mature HECs. In mature HECs,  ID1  was frequently expressed, whereas  ID2  and  ID4  were rarely detected (Supplementary Fig. S8). These findings are broadly consistent with our spatial transcriptomic analysis.    Fig. 4   Endothelial-focused spatial transcriptomic and MIF analyses within TLSs. MIF consistently showed strong ID1 protein staining in the HECs of mature TLSs, although some HECs lacked ID1 staining (Fig.  4 I). Functionally, the adhesion signature for HECs, calculated from PNAd-associated genes, together with  SELE ,  SELP ,  ICAM1 , and  VCAM1 , was significantly higher in mature TLSs than in immature TLSs (Fig.  4 J,  P  < 0.05). In the biomarker validation cohort ( n  = 45), 18 patients (40%) had ID1-high HEVs, whereas the remaining 27 patients (60%) had ID1-low HEVs or lacked mature TLSs (baseline characteristics are summarized in Supplementary Table S3). Patients with tumors with ID1-high HEVs showed a markedly higher objective response rate (61%) compared with those with ID1-low HEVs (17%) or without mature TLSs (7%) (Fig.  4 L,  P  < 0.05). Likewise, Kaplan–Meier analysis showed a pronounced survival advantage among patients with ID1-high HEVs, with median OS not reached versus 21.4 months in the ID1-low HEVs/absent mature TLSs groups (Fig.  4 M, log-rank  P  < 0.001). Furthermore, multivariate analysis identified the presence of ID1-high HEVs as an independent prognostic factor (Table  2 ). Finally, responders and non-responders showed no clear differences in baseline characteristics within the ID1-high group, suggesting the limits of ID1-high HEVs as a predictor (Supplementary Table S4). Together, these data identify ID1-high HEVs as a functional hallmark of mature TLSs and a robust biomarker of enhanced immunotherapy efficacy and survival in NSCLC. UMAP embedding and stacked bar plot reveal that, although the two cohorts harbored a comparable number of TLS (Wilcoxon  p  = 0.88), ICB therapy was associated with a trend toward a more B-cell-dominant intralesional profile (Wilcoxon  p  = 0.11), whereas control TLSs contained B- and T-cell compartments in roughly equal proportions (Fig.  5 A, B). Area-normalized chemokine profiling revealed a treatment-specific dichotomy: control TLSs expressed higher levels of inflammatory  CCL4 ,  CCL18 ,  CCL21  and  CXCL9-11  cluster, whereas ICB-treated TLSs showed selective upregulation of  CXCL12  together with its receptor  CXCR4 .  CXCL13  expression per TLS area remained comparable between groups despite increased  CXCR5  expression in ICB-treated TLSs (Fig.  5 C). TLS-area–normalized cell counts confirmed treatment-specific re-patterning, with increased conventional and follicular B cell densities under ICB therapy, whereas central-proliferating B cells were unchanged and exhibited lower  MKI67  expression. While the number of Tfh cells increased, their  CXCL13  output decreased sharply. Although fibroblast numbers were comparable,  CXCL12  expression increased markedly in the ICB cohort.  CXCR4  levels also increased consistently across these cell types (Fig.  5 D, E). Furthermore, spatial CCI maps demonstrated that TLSs in ICB–treated tumors displayed stronger  CXCL12–CXCR4  signaling than those in untreated controls (Fig.  5 F). Within this pathway, fibroblasts showed the strongest communication probabilities with follicular B cells (Fig.  5 G). Nearest-neighbor distances between fibroblasts and FoBs were comparable in the control and ICB cohort (Fig.  5 H). Among the fibroblast subsets, PDGFRA⁺ fibroblasts were identified as the population most likely to interact with FoBs through the CXCL12–CXCR4 axis (Supplementary Fig. S9) [ 37 ]. High  CXCL12  expression within TLSs has been proposed to correlate with greater immune-cell infiltration and favor antitumor activity [ 38 ]. Consistent with this notion, patients with NSCLC treated with immunotherapy for tumors harboring CXCL12-high TLSs showed a significantly longer OS compared with those with CXCL12-low or TLS-negative tumors (median OS 60.2 vs. 26.6 months; log-rank  P  = 0.014) (Fig.  5 I, J). In summary, immunotherapy-driven tumor regression enhanced  CXCL12–CXCR4  signaling, suggesting that patients with TLSs bearing this  CXCL12 -high niche may have a greater survival benefit from ICB therapy. ICB–treated tumors contained fewer PNAd-positive HEV per square millimeter than control, indicating a treatment-related reduction in HEV density (Fig.  6 A, B). TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors exhibited a transcriptional shift in which adhesion genes including  SELE  and  SELP  together with the PNAd-biosynthetic module — B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1  and  ST3GAL4 — were likewise suppressed, and the differentiation brake  ID1  fell sharply, along with  ID2  (Fig.  6 C, D). In contrast, angio-remodeling transcripts, including  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  VEGFA ,  APLN ,  APLNR , and  FLT1 , increased. However, VEGFA expression within endothelial cells was minimal, and the ligand was predominantly supplied by fibroblasts rather than by HEVs themselves (Supplementary Fig. 10). Gene Ontology analysis consistently shows that ICB therapy redirected HECs from an immune-recruitment program toward vascular remodeling: genes that are upregulated in the treated group clustered within angiogenesis pathways, whereas those enriched in controls were related to immune trafficking (Fig.  6 E). Furthermore, ICB therapy significantly decreased an adhesion signature per TLS, defined by  B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1 ,  ST3GAL4 ,  SELE ,  SELP ,  ICAM1  and  VCAM1 , while simultaneously amplifying an angio-remodel signature comprising  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  APLN ,  APLNR ,  FLT1  and  TEK  (Fig.  6 F, G). Functionally, the normalized counts of conventional B, CD4⁺ T, and CD8⁺ T cells located within 100 μm of a HEC were significantly reduced in the ICB cohort (Fig.  6 H,  P  < 0.05). Finally, MIF showed markedly reduced ID1 protein in TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors compared with controls, mirroring the transcriptomic downregulation described above (Fig.  6 I, J). In summary, TLS-associated HEVs potentially shift phenotypically with TLS maturation and treatment. In immature TLS, HEVs first express the LTβR axis and homing chemokines, recruiting lymphocytes via nascent HEC cuffs with BECs. During maturation,  ID1  increases, and classical adhesion features together with the PNAd-synthetic enzyme set predominates, yielding a fully functional “mature HEV.” ICB ultimately regresses tumors and drives the vessels into a remodeled endothelial state: ID1 levels fall sharply, the adhesion/PNAd module contracts, and lymphocyte influx diminishes, while vascular-remodeling genes are induced, preserving structural plasticity (Fig.  6 K). ( I ) Representative MIF illustrating ID1 level in TLS HEVs from control and ICB-treated tumors. ( J ) Quantification of ID1-positive HECs per TLS (mean of counts from three representative fields).  (K)  Schematic summarizing endothelial transitions in TLS from immature HEV ( LTβR -rich) to mature HEV ( ID1 -high, adhesion/PNAd-rich) and, after ICB therapy, to remodeled HEV ( ID1 -low, vascular remodeling–associated transcriptomes-upregulated)                      Discussion  TLSs are promising biomarkers for stratifying cancer patients undergoing immunotherapy, whereas their detailed biology, especially at the endothelial level, remains poorly characterized. In the present study, we aimed to map how TLS composition and endothelial dynamics varied with maturation and treatment, and link these mechanistic insights to clinical outcomes to elucidate their contribution to TLS-mediated antitumor immunity.  This study provides an integrated spatial-omics framework unifying the cellular and clinical dimensions of TLSs in NSCLC, particularly in endothelial populations. By combining high-sensitivity in situ transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence, and immunotherapy-related clinical outcomes, we delineate three key principles: (i) TLS maturation establishes novel immune niches in NSCLC, (ii) ID1-high HEVs within mature TLSs confer clinical benefit, and (iii) ICB therapy reprograms HEVs from a lymphocyte-recruiting phenotype to a vascular-reprogramming state while enhancing a  CXCL12-CXCR4  niche.  Spatial transcriptomics is indispensable for analyzing TLS biology. TLSs juxtapose lymphoid, myeloid, and stromal elements in complex three-dimensional assemblies. Therefore, only methods that preserve tissue coordinates and resolve individual cells can reveal their true organization. The Xenium In Situ platforms provide sub-micrometer, in-situ detection of transcripts, enabling the visual validation of cell annotations and tracking of follicles, vessels, and related microstructure continuity throughout an entire TLS. By applying this platform, we profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells at single-cell resolution to obtain a nearly exhaustive annotation of every anatomical component. We further expanded the standard immuno-oncology panel with vascular-specific genes, allowing cytokine and chemokine quantification across all cell types, with a focus on endothelial cells.  Consistent with our observations, studies in both hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer show that mature TLSs are characterized by  CXCL13 -rich, B-cell-dominated cores, whereas immature aggregates show enrichment of  CXCL9-11  and Th1-skewed signatures [ 23 ,  39 ]. While single-cell studies on HEVs in human tumors are limited, analogous analyses in human lymph nodes are increasing [ 30 ,  40 ]. These nodal datasets have demonstrated that PNAd-positive HEVs form a discrete endothelial cluster characterized by high expression of adhesion genes such as  SELE ,  SELP ,  B3GNT3  and  CHST4 , whereas BECs segregate as a separate population lacking immune-trafficking functions. These observations are consistent with our findings, supporting the conclusion that TLS maturation is conserved across different organs and tumor types.  ID1 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcriptional regulator lacking a DNA-binding motif. Instead, it heterodimerizes with canonical bHLH factors, blocking lineage-specific transcription and sustaining a proliferative, undifferentiated state. Its expression is induced by a variety of upstream cues, including BMP/SMAD1-5, TGF-β, VEGF-A/VEGFR2, hypoxia-stabilized HIF-1α, Wnt/β-catenin, and inflammatory cytokines [ 41 ]. In tumors,  ID1  is enriched mainly in malignant and endothelial cells and promotes metastasis and angiogenesis; therefore, its overexpression correlates with poor prognosis. However, its involvement in HEVs remains unreported [ 42 ]. Lyden et al. showed that physiological  ID  expression is indispensable for angiogenesis in  ID  knockout mouse models, in which endothelial cells lacking  ID1  emerged in tumor xenografts but did not lumenize or generate properly branched vessels [ 43 ]. Accordingly, ID family genes are critical for synchronizing endothelial differentiation with the invasive expansion of the vascular network. Typically, high  ID1  expression in bulk lung tumor tissue is linked to poor prognosis, whereas our data show that within TLSs, elevated  ID1  levels trend toward improved clinical outcomes [ 44 ]. Such  ID1 -like “context-dependent inversions” are likewise observed for several other genes within the TLS compartment. Although the  CXCL12–CXCR4  axis is classically pro-tumorigenic outside TLSs, promoting metastasis, angiogenesis, and immune evasion through ERK1/2, Ras, p38 MAPK, PLC/MAPK, and JNK cascades [ 45 ], CXCL12 expression in combined hepatocellular–cholangiocarcinoma correlates positively with TLS density, TLS maturation, and favorable prognosis, suggesting that within TLSs this axis may instead support lymphoid organization and maturation [ 38 ]. In parallel, a recent study in hepatocellular carcinoma demonstrated that chemotherapy-induced TLS formation is likewise driven by CXCL12–CXCR4–mediated recruitment of immune and stromal cells, further reinforcing the notion that this axis can acquire a TLS-promoting role in specific therapeutic contexts [ 46 ]. Collectively, these observations highlight that signaling pathways traditionally viewed as oncogenic can adopt distinct, TLS-restricted functions, underscoring the need to dissect TLS-specific vascular pathways when developing HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.  CXCL13 is a recognized marker of follicular TLS cores and favorable outcome [ 14 ,  47 ]. In our data, the CXCL13 load per TLS was comparable between the control and ICB-treated cohorts, whereas CXCR5 expression was increased in ICB-treated TLSs. This dissociation suggests that ICB does not globally amplify CXCL13 production itself, but rather selectively enhances the responsiveness of B cells and Tfh to a relatively stable CXCL13 field. By contrast, knowledge regarding chemokines other than CXCL13 remains limited. Our data show that ICB selectively augments  CXCL12  expression in fibroblasts. Although the mechanistic link between PD-1 signaling and  CXCL12  induction remains to be elucidated, the increase in CXCL12 parallels a modest association between PD-L1 TPS and TLS maturation [ 13 ]. Consistent with independent spatial omics studies, mature TLSs displayed strikingly high  CXCL12  levels, mirroring the  CXCL13  pattern, suggesting that, in this compartmentalized niche,  CXCL12  may emerge as a biomarker of durable benefits in immunotherapy-treated patients rather than a canonical pro-tumorigenic signal [ 38 ]. Nevertheless, multivariate models incorporating TLS maturation as a confounder did not identify CXCL12 as an independent predictor, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation. In contrast, ID1 retained its independent prognostic significance even after adjustment, despite possible unmeasured immunosuppressive factors limiting its predictive value. Although our study is retrospective and does not allow longitudinal tracking of individual HEVs, one possible interpretation is that an ID1-high, functionally active HEV niche is well established at baseline in tumors that ultimately respond to ICB. In contrast, such an ID1-high niche may be insufficiently formed or inadequately maintained in non-responders. These post-treatment changes do not contradict the prognostic relevance of baseline ID1-high HEVs. Baseline ID1-high HEVs in untreated tumors reflect a reactive, lymphocyte-recruiting program that facilitates antitumor immunity and predicts ICI benefit, similar to reports showing that pre-existing HEV-rich tumors are associated with improved clinical outcomes [ 48 ]. In contrast, the ID1-low, PNAd-low, angiogenic-signature–high state observed after ICI likely represents a physiological reprogramming process during the resolution of inflammation, in which HEVs transition from a recruitment-competent phenotype to a vascular-maintenance or retention-type state. Thus, the baseline predictive role of ID1 and its post-therapy reduction correspond to distinct temporal phases of HEV biology rather than opposing biological effects. In summary, our work illustrates ID1 as a novel predictive and monitoring biomarker, although its regulatory mechanisms require further research.  The principal strength of this study was the application of Xenium In Situ, which preserved the native continuity of TLSs and their vasculature while providing single-cell resolution. Conventional scRNA-seq–derived “TLS-mimic” datasets cannot attain this fidelity: our approach profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells and retained intact follicles and vessels, which allowed the direct assessment of CCIs and HEV-mediated lymphocyte recruitment. We then validated the markers identified through this spatial screening in independent immunotherapy cohorts, thereby establishing ID1 as a clinically relevant biomarker associated with survival. However, the study has several limitations. First, the target-gene panel was relatively small. Although the default set captures core cell-type markers, it does not include essential TLS genes such as  BCL6  and  AICDA , which should be custom-added for deeper analyses. Second, the discovery and validation cohorts were modest in size and retrospective in design; thus, selection bias was possible, and the generalizability of the findings is limited. To address these issues, a prospective study with a larger patient cohort is warranted.  In conclusion, our data revealed a link between TLS maturation or ICB therapy and HEC differentiation, in which  ID1  plays a pivotal regulatory role. In mature TLSs, HECs display high  ID1  expression, actively recruit lymphocytes, and are associated with favorable clinical outcomes. However, after ICB induced tumor regressions,  ID1  and adhesion transcripts in HECs decreased sharply, lymphocyte ingress wanes, and a vascular remodeling-signature was induced. Therefore, ID1 has emerged as a dynamic biomarker in patients treated with immunotherapy. Collectively, these findings provide a mechanistic framework and a practical biomarker set for HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.    Supplementary Information

evidence_text:
High-definition spatial transcriptomic profiling of immune cell populations in colorectal cancer. A comprehensive understanding of cellular behavior and response to the tumor microenvironment (TME) in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains elusive. Here, we introduce the high-definition Visium spatial transcriptomic technology (Visium HD) and investigate formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded human CRC samples (n = 5). We demonstrate the high sensitivity, single-cell-scale resolution and spatial accuracy of Visium HD, generating a highly refined whole-transcriptome spatial profile of CRC samples. We identify transcriptomically distinct macrophage subpopulations in different spatial niches with potential pro-tumor and anti-tumor functions via interactions with tumor and T cells. In situ gene expression analysis validates our findings and localizes a clonally expanded T cell population close to macrophages with anti-tumor features. Our study demonstrates the power of high-resolution spatial technologies to understand cellular interactions in the TME and paves the way for larger studies that will unravel mechanisms and biomarkers of CRC biology, improving diagnosis and disease management strategies. Main  CRC accounted for 9.4% of cancer-related deaths (0.9 million) in 2020, and its global incidence is predicted to double by 2035 (refs.   1 , 2  ). Its poor 5-year survival rate highlights the need for better early detection and prognostic biomarkers for future disease management  3  . Growing evidence suggests that tumor heterogeneity is best described at the transcriptome level, rather than with classical histopathological or mutation-centered disease classifications  4  . Technologies that refine our understanding of the TME, including the diverse roles of innate and adaptive immune responses and cellular crosstalk in CRC, have the potential to inform better clinical intervention strategies.  Sequencing-based genomic technologies have played an important role in building our knowledge of CRC biology  4 – 7  . However, bulk sequencing, which involves averages data from cells and tissues, is confounded by the complexities of the TME and intratumor heterogeneity. Single-cell transcriptomic (single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq)) technologies have partially filled this gap and allowed for detailed exploration of the cell types within the TME in CRC  8 – 16  . Although these studies add critical single-cell-level resolution to our understanding of CRC, they lack any information about the cellular organization within the tissue. Spatial transcriptomics offers a solution. Several commercial technologies are currently available, including Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium v2’, 10x Genomics), STOmics (BGI) and Curio Seeker (Curio Bioscience). Other published methods include Seq-Scope  17  , Nova-ST  18  , Open-ST  19  , HDST  20  , DBiT-seq  21  , Pixel-seq  22   and XYZeq  23  . These methods have enabled the localization of cell types within tissues, which is critical for understanding the interaction between cells in the TME of CRC  24 – 27  . However, these technologies lack resolution at the single-cell scale or are typically only compatible with freshly frozen tissues, and, as such, a deep understanding of tumor organization based on readily available biobanked samples remains elusive.  Here, we introduce Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium HD’), a whole-transcriptome assay with single-cell-scale resolution compatible with freshly frozen, fixed frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples. The Visium HD slides provide a dramatically increased oligonucleotide barcode density (~11,000,000 continuous 2-µm features in a 6.5 × 6.5-mm Visium HD capture area, compared to ~5,000 55-µm features with gaps between the equivalent Visium v2 capture area), generating data that can be binned in square features. We demonstrate the use of Visium HD as a discovery platform by profiling CRC FFPE tissue blocks from multiple patients. The single-cell-scale resolution of Visium HD allowed us to map distinct populations of immune cells, specifically macrophages and T cells, and evaluate DGE at the tumor boundary. We also generated a multi-patient single-cell reference dataset from a larger cohort of FFPE samples and used it to annotate deconvolved Visium HD data bins, validating the cell type populations identified by Visium HD and subsequently using the integrated data to comprehensively map the cellular composition and molecular signatures of the TME in CRC. Leveraging the high resolution of Visium HD, we examined the cells at the immediate periphery (within 50 µm) of the tumor. This allowed us to spatially map distinct macrophage subpopulations to specific tumor regions, to compare their transcriptomic profiles, which indicate that they may exert pro-tumor roles via different pathways, and to characterize cell–cell interactions. To validate the spatial accuracy of Visium HD, we analyzed a subset of genes using an independent spatial technology (Xenium In Situ Gene Expression  28  ). We confirmed the presence of the two pro-tumor macrophage subpopulations in different tumor niches and pinpointed the location of the T cells within the TME. We also detected a clonally expanded T cell population and the microenvironment in which it resides, revealing a macrophage-containing niche with anti-tumor features.  Our study underscores the importance of using high-resolution spatial technologies in exploring the heterogeneity of cancer biology. These advanced tools are crucial for precisely mapping diverse immune cell niches and elucidating the complex interactions between these cells and their microenvironment. Spatial technologies provide a detailed understanding of spatial variations in cell types, their subpopulations and cell-to-cell relationships, which are key to developing targeted therapies and personalized treatment approaches. The combination of whole-transcriptome and targeted in situ spatial technologies used in our investigation provides a deep insight into the complex and dynamic nature of the TME, highlighting the importance of spatial context in understanding cancer heterogeneity and disease progression.    Results  Visium HD enables transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression analysis at single-cell scale. Gene expression is measured by the capture of ligated probe pairs targeting the whole protein-coding transcriptome. We profiled tumor biopsies from five patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma, in addition to normal adjacent tissue (NAT) from three of these patients (Table  1 ). Serial sections of FFPE tissues were used to benchmark the technology performance or to explore the TME using Visium HD. Additionally, selected serial sections were used to generate an scRNA-seq dataset and for in situ gene expression analysis (Fig.  1 ). Visium HD specifications and performance  The Visium HD capture array consists of 2 × 2-µm squares of uniquely barcoded oligonucleotides directly adjacent to each other on the slide, resulting in a continuous lawn of capture oligonucleotides. This represents an increase of several orders of magnitude in barcode complexity over earlier Visium slides, which have 55-µm circular capture areas with a 100-µm center to center gaps between them (Fig.  2a,b ). For downstream analysis, the Space Ranger (version 3.0) pipeline outputs the raw 2-µm data and data binned at 8- and 16-µm resolution. Unless otherwise described, we used the 8-µm binned data in our analyses.                    The estimated fraction of molecules arising from off-target probe binding events, that is, probes binding to genomic DNA (gDNA), was reduced in Visium HD (average of 4.13% in Visium v2 and 0.70% in Visium HD) (Supplementary Table  1 ). To assess any potential bias arising from such events, these probes were computationally excluded for this analysis, after which we observed a stronger correlation between the UMI counts from the different assays ( R  2  = 0.92, Fig.  2d ;  R  2  = 0.93 and 0.96, Extended Data Fig.  1 ).  In array-based spatial technologies, the analyte to be measured (messenger RNA (mRNA) itself or a ligated probe reporting on the mRNA) must move from the tissue to come in contact with the array. Precise transfer of analytes with minimal lateral movement is essential to ensure that the spatial transcript measurements are representative of the biology of the tissue being analyzed. To achieve this, tissue placement and subsequent molecular biology reactions must be carefully controlled to minimize lateral movement of transcripts or their proxies away from the site of origin. Similar to the Visium v2 assay, Visium HD uses the CytAssist instrument. The CytAssist controls reagent flow and thus allows target molecules from the tissue to be captured upon release, preventing free diffusion of transcripts and ensuring accurate transfer of analytes from tissues to the capture arrays. The spatial fidelity gains afforded by the CytAssist have been described previously  29 , 30   (technical note  CG000618 , revision B). To quantify the spatial accuracy of Visium HD, we analyzed genes with distinct localization to the glands of normal colon mucosal tissue (goblet cell gene markers:  CLCA1 ,  FCGBP  and  MUC2 ). In each tissue section, we manually selected four regions of interest (ROIs) and, for each marker gene, quantified the number of UMIs that were within or outside of the annotated structures in which their expression is expected based on established expression patterns  31  . We observed that most transcripts (98.3–99%) were localized in their expected morphological locations within the source masks, and only a small proportion (0.97–1.73%) were in adjacent masks (Fig.  2e  and Extended Data Fig.  2 ), consistent with faithful transfer of ligated probes from the tissue to the array at single-cell-scale resolution.
