Graphical abstract Keywords acute interstitial nephritis ICI-AKI immune checkpoint inhibitor interferon gamma JAK-STAT1 spatial transcriptomics pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND ICIs, which target programmed death (PD)-1, PD-ligand 1 (PD-L1), cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein-4, and lymphocyte activation gene-3, release the brakes on the immune system and enhance its ability to destroy tumor cells. These drugs, which are now approved to treat > 20 cancer types, have dramatically improved outcomes for a number of malignancies. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 AKI is common in the setting of ICIs, with real-world studies showing that 15% to 25% of patients treated with ICIs develop AKI. 5 Although AIN is the most common histopathologic lesion seen in ICI-AKI, 6 , 7 AKI can also occur because of non-ICI-related causes, including ATN. Distinguishing ICI-AIN from ICI-ATN is challenging without a kidney biopsy, because there are no clinical features specific to ICI-AIN. 6 Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying ICI-AIN are not well understood. Recent studies have shown that proinflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis factor, IFN-γ, and IFN-γ-induced chemokines such as CXCL 9, 10, and 11 are elevated in ICI-AIN but not in patients treated with ICI with AKI from other causes. 8 , 9 , 10 Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of tissue from patients with ICI-colitis 11 and myocarditis 12 have each identified an immune cell infiltration dominated by T cells and inflammatory myeloid cells, in addition to organ-specific differences, such as interleukin-17A-producing T cells in ICI-colitis. In contrast to ICI-colitis and ICI-myocarditis, our understanding of the immune cell infiltrate, cellular interactions, and damage pathways in ICI-AIN is limited. Given the expanding indications for ICIs, the burden of disease of ICI-AIN is expected to increase. 13 , 14 New insights into underlying mechanisms are urgently needed to improve the identification of at-risk patients, enable noninvasive diagnosis of ICI-AIN, and identify new therapeutic targets without inhibiting the antitumor response. Here, we utilized Xenium Prime 5K (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA), a novel spatial transcriptomics technology, to compare and contrast the cellular composition of kidney biopsy specimens from patients with ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN. Methods Patient Selection and Tissue Collection We identified adult patients (≥ 18 years old) at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and/or Dana-Farber Cancer Institute who had received at least 1 dose of ICI therapy within 180 days before development of AKI (defined as a ≥ 1.5-fold rise in serum creatinine from pre-ICI baseline) 15 and who had a kidney biopsy performed for clinical purposes between 2021 and 2024. A total of 8 archival formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded kidney biopsies were obtained (4 with moderate-to-severe AIN and 4 with ATN, as adjudicated by 2 renal pathologists at Brigham and Women’s Hospital). All patients had consented to blood and urine collection, as well as archival tissue collection. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of archival tissue was conducted under institutional review board approved protocol (#2023P000393). Additionally, all patients had available urine proteomics data (Olink Target 96 Immuno-Oncology Panel and Olink Target 96 inflammation, with 140 unique proteins; Olink Proteomics, Uppsala, Sweden), as previously described. 8 This study was approved by the Brigham and Women’s Hospital and/or Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (21-685) and Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Boards (#2021P00044 and #2023P000393). Xenium Slide Preparation Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks of kidney biopsies were sliced onto Xenium slides according to the “Xenium In Situ for Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded-Tissue Preparation Guide” ( CG000578 Rev C, 10x Genomics) 16 protocol. The Xenium slides were then prepared following the “Xenium In Situ for Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded-Deparaffinization and Decrosslinking” protocol ( CG000580 Rev D, 10x Genomics). In brief, the slides were incubated at 60 °C for 30 minutes and then sequentially immersed in xylene, ethanol, and nuclease-free water to deparaffinize and rehydrate the tissue. The Xenium slides were then immediately incubated in the decrosslinking and permeabilization solution at 80 °C for 30 minutes, followed by a wash with phosphate-buffered saline. The Xenium slides were then processed according to the “Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression” user guide ( CG000760 Rev A, 10x Genomics) for the remaining slide preparation steps. The samples were hybridized with probes from Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue & Pathways Panel (PN-1000671, 10x Genomics) at 50 °C for 18 hours. After hybridization, the slides were washed and incubated with a ligation reaction mix, followed by another wash step and DNA amplification. Cell segmentation staining was then performed, and the slides were treated with an autofluorescence quencher and , 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole before loading into the Xenium instrument. Xenium Analyzer Setup and Data Acquisition Processed Xenium slides were loaded in the Xenium analyzer and imaged, following the guidelines in the “Xenium Analyzer User Guide ( CG000584 Rev F, 10x Genomics).” After scanning, the Xenium slides were removed from the Xenium analyzer and processed with post-run hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining according to the “Xenium In Situ Gene Expression-Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining” protocol ( CG000613 Rev A, 10x Genomics). Xenium Data Analysis We performed both image-based segmentation using CellPose 17 and transcripts-based cell segmentation using Baysor (v0.7.1) 18 with the previous cell labels from the multimodal staining information. Then, we integrated the Xenium data with single cell RNA-seq reference atlas through Harmony and projected the labels using nearest neighbors, which are further curated with licensed nephrologists. Spatial domain clustering analyses were performed using the natural boundaries-based method, Tessera. 19 Niches were further identified using the de novo clustering analysis and manual curation, and further validated with the approximate positions of tissues on the H&E imaging. Downstream data analysis is described in more detail in the Supplementary Methods . Using Olink Data to Refine Transcriptomics Analyses Using Olink data, we focused on proteins that we had previously shown to be differentially abundant in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN. 8 , 20 For proteins that were included in both the Inflammation and Immuno-Oncology panel, we used the results from the Inflammation panel. We performed pseudo-bulk aggregation of the transcripts per kidney biopsy by the AggregateExpression function in Seurat (v5.3.0) 21 and normalized expression levels to the biopsy area. Results Study Design and Cohort Description We analyzed kidney biopsies of 4 patients with ICI-AIN and 4 with ICI-ATN using the Xenium Prime 5K (10x Genomics) spatial transcriptomics assay to measure in situ expression of 5001 genes ( Figure 1 a). Patients with ICI-ATN were chosen as the comparator, because they share potential confounders (malignant disease, cancer treatment, and unspecific kidney tissue changes caused by AKI); in the ICI-ATN cases, treatment with ICIs was not judged to be the cause of the AKI and often an alternative etiology was identified. Baseline demographics and characteristics of the AKI event are shown in Supplementary Table S1 . Additional information on the kidney biopsy characteristics can be found in Supplementary Table S2 . The time between AKI onset and kidney biopsy ranged from 2 to 18 days (median 7.5 days); all biopsies showed mild-moderate signs of irreversible damage and fibrosis (interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy range 10–40%). Figure 1 Spatial transcriptomics identifies distinct cell states in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN. (a) Study design and techniques involved. (b) Marker heatmap for the major cell types in spatial transcriptomic data. Rows show the cell types, columns show top selected markers, the size. (c) UMAP of spatial transcriptomic cells with cell type annotation in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, the size of the circle indicates the proportion of cells expressing the marker, the color indicates the average expression scale. (d) Differential abundance of cellular composition measured by ratio over all cells for both groups. (e) Cell type ratio in all patients of ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, with corresponding color legend below. (f) Xenium cells from a representative patient with ICI-AIN. (g) Zoomed-in regions from F; multiple polygons show the segmented cells in their spatial position; colors of the polygons show the cell type; white dots with different shapes show the transcript positions. ICI-AIN, Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy-related acute interstitial nephritis; ICI-ATN, ICI therapy-related acute tubular necrosis; pDC, plasmacytoid dendritic cell; cDC1, conventional dendritic cell type 1; Collecting Duct-PC, (principal cells); Collecting Duct-IC, (intercalated cell); Immune (LowQ), Immune cell lineage cells with low quality data. Immune Cells in ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN After cell segmentation and quality control ( Supplementary Figure S1 ), followed by label transfer and manual curation strategy, we identified a total of 332,341 cells (79% kept cells after quality control of resegmentation) with 21,251 to 66,751 cells per patient sample ( Supplementary Figure S1 ). Using curated cell types from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project atlas as a reference, we took 4875 overlapping high-quality genes between Xenium and Kidney Precision Medicine Project single-cell RNA-sequencing and jointly clustered the cells to define 24 major cell types. These cell types comprised both kidney parenchymal cells and immune cells across all 8 patient samples, expressing known biomarkers. The alignment performed well at the major lineage level ( Figure 1 b–c, Supplementary Figure S1 ), as we observed high correlation of gene expression fold changes between the Kidney Precision Medicine Project atlas and our Xenium datasets ( Supplementary Figure S2–3 ), although the cell segmentation of cell types with complex, nonspheroidal geometries also led to spillover of transcripts into neighboring cells (e.g., in glomerular cell types). Next, we applied covarying neighborhood analysis 22 to identify cell states strongly associated with ICI-AIN and found immune cells to be significantly expanded in ICI-AIN (global P -value 0.02, Figure 1 d). Compared with ICI-ATN, on average, ICI-AIN biopsies contained 27-fold more XBP high plasma cells in ICI-AIN, 8-fold more IL3RA + plasmacytoid dendritic cells, 7.9-fold more proliferating T cells, 7.6-fold more FOXP3 + CTLA4 + regulatory T cells (Tregs), and 3.6-fold more CXCL9 + CIITA + inflammatory myeloid cells ( Figure 1 e, Supplementary Figure S1 , false discovery rate < 0.05 for each). We also identified more kidney parenchymal cells in ICI-ATN, including SCNN1G+ collecting duct cells (2.2-fold higher), PODXL + podocytes (3.4-fold higher), KCNJ10 + distal convoluted tubular cells (2.3-fold higher), and CUBN + proximal tubular cells (2.1-fold higher), likely influenced by the variable sampling of kidney medulla during biopsies ( Supplementary Table S2 ). By mapping the cell types and individual detected marker transcripts in space, we were able to confirm the identified cell types in their spatial context, including high levels of CD19 and CD3E transcripts in a large lymphoid aggregate, PODXL transcripts in glomeruli, and CUBN in proximal tubular cells ( Figure 1 f–g). In summary, we were able to characterize the immune cell infiltrate in ICI-AIN using spatial transcriptomics and identified a high density of plasma cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and T cells, among others. Immune and Fibrosis Niches in ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN To dissect cellular neighborhoods in their spatial context, we identified cellular niches using the Tessera package. 19 Tessera is an automated tissue-agnostic tissue segmentation method that introduces novel concepts of spatial cellular neighborhoods, or “niches,” delineates the tissues by closed multipolygons that aggregate spatially coherent cells, and approaches that infer the tissues’ edge with natural tissue boundaries. Tessera enables reducing the sparsity of spatial transcriptomic data and circumvents potential problems associated with cell segmentation methods by aggregating cells, thereby increasing the number of relevant transcripts per unit and decreasing misattribution errors. Using Tessera to characterize cellular niches in these biopsies, our approach enables us to identify potentially novel cellular niches and biologically meaningful architectural units within the spatial transcriptomic data. In total, we aggregated cells to 22,690 niches. Based on the clustering of these niches based on transcriptional similarities, we defined 9 major spatial niches, including immune, vascular, and fibrotic niches, and 6 kidney tissue-related niches ( Figure 2 a–d). Figure 2 Immune and stromal cellular niches are expanded in ICI-AIN. ( a) UMAP projection of niches using the aggregated gene expression in ICI-AIN patient group; each dot represents a tile with color showing different annotation of niche type. (b) UMAP for cells in ICI-ATN patient group, the legend as in A. (c) Heatmap of cell type ratio in each spatial niche, annotated color bar legend is the same as in A, the cell colors show the abundance of the cell type ratio. (d) Dot heatmap plot showing the marker average expression and expressed tile percentage. (e) multipolygon plot visualizes the spatial niches of one representative ICI-AIN patient, (f). same as E but for a patient with ICI-ATN. (g–h) marker expression in spatial niches for the same patient in E and F. (i) UMAP rendering which is colored by the covarying neighborhood analysis of spatial niches comparing ICI-AIN to ICI-ATN, red represents the increased niche abundance in ICI-AIN, blue depicts lower abundance. (j) UMAP showing the VCAM1+ niches across the 8 patients. The kidney-related niches included all major parts of the nephron—for example, glomerular niches were marked by high expression of PODXL and WT1 . Similarly, we identified niches corresponding to the proximal tubule (with high expression of CUBN and LRP2 ), loop of Henle (marked by UMOD and CASR expression), distal convoluted tubule (marked by TRPM6 expression), and collecting duct (expressing SCNN1G and HSD11B2 and combining both intercalated and principal cells; Figure 2 d). Additionally, we identified niches associated with pathology; injured proximal tubular regions were marked by the expression of markers like HAVCR1 (encoding kidney injury molecule 1) and SOX9 in addition to the proximal tubule transcriptional signature, as has been extensively studied in the context of AKI. 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 Immune niches contained different immune cell subsets; generally, we identified high levels of IFN-γ-induced transcripts like SLAMF7 , CD38, and CXCL9 . Similarly, areas of fibrosis were marked by high expression of genes like PDGFRA and COL5A1 . The identity of the niches was confirmed by their cellular composition ( Figure 2 c), with the spatial expression of key marker genes following accurate niche distribution ( Figure 2 e–h). We then applied covarying neighborhood analysis to characterize the cellular niches that were significantly expanded in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN (global P -value 0.03). We observed an expansion of immune fibrotic niches, as well as niches containing loop of Henle transcriptional profile in ICI-AIN, whereas the remaining kidney-specific niches were decreased in ICI-AIN ( Figure 2 i). The injured proximal tubule niche was more highly represented in ICI-ATN samples as marked by VCAM1+ niches ( Figure 2 j). Using a niche-based approach, we were thus able to identify all major parts of the nephron in addition to immune cell and fibrotic niches. Immune Niche Subtyping Identifies Key Immunological Processes in ICI-AIN To better understand the immune cell infiltration in ICI-AIN, we performed unbiased subclustering of the immune niches ( Figure 3 a). We confirmed key features of the ICI-ATN and ICI-AIN histopathology in serial sections ( Supplementary Figure S4 ). Some niches corresponded to the microenvironment of specific immune cells, such as plasma cell niches with high levels of transcripts as FCRL5 and TNFRSF17 (encoding B-cell maturation antigen) or plasmacytoid dendritic cells (expressing LIL4RA , and IL3RA [encoding CD123]) ( Figure 3 b). The tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS)-like niches showed high expression of genes that are involved in the interaction of B and T cells, such as CD28 and ICOS , as well as their component cells. Other niches showed stronger transcriptional signals of the infiltrated kidney tissue or fibrotic processes in addition to an immune cell signature (termed “CD8 infiltrated kidney” and “inflammation with fibrosis”). We detected 2 separate types of myeloid cell niches, one with higher expression of proinflammatory genes (like CSF2RB and MMP9 ) that are often associated with monocyte-derived cells, which we termed “myeloid inflammation,” and another myeloid niche type with increased expression of transcripts associated with tissue-resident or regulatory myeloid cells (such as CD163 , MRC1 which encodes CD206, and F13A1 ). Notably, T cell-related transcripts such as CD3E and CD8A were detected in all immune niches to varying degrees, highlighting the role of T-cell infiltration as a general feature of ICI-AIN. Figure 3 Distinct immune niche subtypes in ICI-AIN. (a) UMAP projection of subclusters in ICI-AIN. (b) Marker genes of immune cell subclusters. (c) Absolute abundance of immune cell type per biopsy. (d) Covariate estimates of the sccomp model of niche composition. A positive slope value indicates a positive association with ICI-AIN. Blue color indicates variates passing the significance threshold ( P < 0.05). (e) Dot plot of selected chemokine receptor/ligand pairs expressed in immune subniches. (f) spatial projection of immune subniches and the CXCR5/CXCL13 and CXCR3/CXCL9 chemokine axes. Compared with ICI-ATN, all immune niche subtypes were increased in ICI-AIN ( Figure 3 c). In a linear regression model examining the association of specific immune niches with ICI-AIN, all immune niche types were increased in ICI-AIN, with the strongest associations observed for the niche types “inflammatory myeloid”, “TLS-like” niches, and “CD8 infiltrated kidney” ( Figure 3 d). There was no association between “inflammatory myeloid” niche abundance and the time between AKI onset and kidney biopsy. Distinct Chemokine Axes Underlie Immune Niche Subtype Heterogeneity To better understand drivers of immune niche heterogeneity, we performed ligand-receptor analysis and observed greater overall ligand-receptor interaction strength across ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN ( Supplementary Figure S5 A and B). In both ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, CXCL12-CXCR4, and CXCL9-CXCR3 interactions were observed in all patients, although the latter pair had higher strengths of association in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN ( Supplementary Figure S5 C–F). CXCL12-CXCR4 was globally present in areas with myeloid inflammation, TLS, and plasma cells in ICI-AIN, whereas it was limited to a few niches in ICI-ATN. Investigating the different immune subniches, expression of CXCR3 ligands CXCL9, 10, and 11 was observed in all subniches, but most prominently in the “myeloid inflammation” niches. This was associated with massive expansion of CXCR3-expressing cells ( Figure 3 e–f, Supplementary Figure S5 G–J). The chemokine axes CCR7 and/or CCL19 and CXCR5 and/or CXCL13, both associated with B-T cell interaction and TLS, were most strongly detected in the TLS-like immune niches. CXCL12 was most strongly increased in plasma cell niches, as has previously been reported in bone marrow plasma cells. 27 Our analyses highlight the role of chemokines in the spatial organization of immune infiltrates in ICI-AIN, with CXCR3-CXCL9 interactions in areas of myeloid inflammation and CXCR5-CXCL13 interactions in TLS. Spatial Transcriptomics Builds on Findings from Urine Proteomics Building upon our previous urine proteomics analysis, 8 we compared paired aggregate gene expression and proteomic abundance of 5 differentially abundant proteins in ICI-AIN (CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, FASLG, GZMA) and 1 in ICI-ATN (epidermal growth factor; Supplementary Figure S6 ). 8 Mean aggregate transcript levels in ICI-AIN for these genes were changed in the same direction as the urinary protein abundance. Gene expression of CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, and GZMA each completely separated the groups, often showing better separation than urine protein levels. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Identifies Interferon-Driven Responses in ICI-AIN We next asked what signaling pathways contribute to the immune cell activation and tissue inflammation in ICI-AIN. Comparing differentially expressed genes within the niche types separately, IFN-γ-induced genes, such as STAT1 and CXCL9, showed the strongest expression in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN in most cellular niches ( Supplementary Figure S7 ). Gene set enrichment analysis of immune-related pathways in the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (RRID:SCR_012773) and Hallmark gene set collections similarly identified an increase in IFN-driven pathways (such as “Interferon gamma response”, “chemokine signaling”, “Janus Kinase-STAT”) in ICI-AIN ( Supplementary Figure S7 ). Especially within the tubular niches, including the injured proximal tubule, collecting duct and loop of Henle, we observed a strong reduction in the expression of genes related to oxidative phosphorylation in ICI-AIN. In summary, the IFN-γ response signature was the dominant transcriptional immune signature in ICI-AIN. Tissue-Resident CD8 + T Cells in ICI-AIN Produce IFN-γ and CXCL13 As we identified IFN-γ and/or STAT1 as the predominant signaling pathway and IFN-γ-induced genes as the top differentially expressed genes in ICI-AIN, we next investigated the cellular source of IFN-γ production. The greatest number of IFNG transcripts (75.1% of all IFNG transcripts identified in immune cells) were identified in CD8 + T cells as compared with other immune cell subsets, including CD4 + T cells ( Figure 4 a). Investigating differentially expressed genes within the CD8 + T cells, we found IFNG to be one of the top upregulated genes in ICI-AIN ( Figure 4 b). CXCL13 was also increased in CD8 + T cells, as were markers of repeated activation, such as PDCD1, LAG3, and CTLA4 in ICI-AIN CD8 + T cells. Although ICI-ATN CD8 + T cells expressed markers of short-lived effector T cells like KLRG1 and CX3CR1 , CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN showed higher levels of residency program markers like ZNF683 (encoding HOBIT), CXCR6, and ITGAE (encoding CD103). Additionally, CD8+ T cells from patients with ICI-AIN were enriched for IFN-induced genes like STAT1 , GBP1, and GBP5. Figure 4 Spatial analysis of IFN gamma response in the immune and fibrotic niche. (a) Percentage of different immune cell subsets among all immune cells with IFNG transcripts detectable. (b) Volcano plot of differentially expressed genes among CD8+ T cells comparing ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN. (c) Gene module score for “Oxidative Phosphorylation” at the niche level. ∗∗∗: P < 0.001 in Mann-Whitney U test. (d) Pearson correlation between gene module scores for “Oxidative Phosphorylation” and “IFNg Response” in proximal tubule niches from patients with ICI-AIN. (e) Feature plot UMAP of the “IFNg Response” module score mapped on immune niches. Red dashed lines indicate the “proinflammatory myeloid cell” niches. Smaller feature plots show gene expression levels of MMP9 and IDO1 , marker genes of proinflammatory myeloid cells. (f) Violin plot of the “IFNg Response” module score shown for different immune niches. (g) Likelihood of directly neighboring a fibrosis niche shown for different immune niches. Each dot represents one sample; the dash shows the mean per condition. (h) Violin plot of the “Fibrotic Niche” module score shown for different immune niches. As identified by gene set enrichment analysis, gene expression relating to oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in ICI-AIN samples, and tubular epithelial cells rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation because of their high energy demand. 28 Using the spatial niche data, we found this reduction localized mostly to the niches related to parts of the kidney tubule ( Figure 4 c). The gene module score for oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in the injured as compared with the noninjured proximal tubule niches. However, in both injured and healthy proximal tubule niches in AIN samples, there was an additive reduction in oxidative phosphorylation gene signatures in multivariable linear regression models ( Supplementary Figure S8 ). IFN-γ-signaling within the noninjured proximal tubule niches was strongly anticorrelated with a gene signature for oxidative phosphorylation ( Figure 4 d). Another hallmark effect of IFN-γ is the polarization of myeloid cells into a proinflammatory, tissue-aggressive state, as we observed in the “inflammatory myeloid” cluster ( Figure 3 a–b). 29 Within this cluster, we found the expression of genes typical for a proinflammatory myeloid polarization (such as MMP9 , IDO1 ), as well as the highest gene expression signature of an IFN-γ response ( Figure 4 e–f). In summary, CD8 + T cell-derived IFN-γ was associated with reduced oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells and a proinflammatory signature in inflammatory myeloid cells. Tissue-Resident Macrophage Niches Associate With Fibrosis Finally, we investigated which immune cell niches were associated with fibrosis in ICI-AIN. To this end, we calculated the probability of neighboring an area of fibrosis for each subtype of immune niche, normalized for the relative abundance of immune niches. The CD8+ infiltrated and tissue-resident myeloid cell niches in ICI-AIN were most likely to neighbor fibrotic niches compared with the ICI-ATN group ( Figure 4 g). Additionally, we defined a fibrotic niche transcriptional signature as the top 100 differentially expressed genes for the fibrosis niches and calculated a signature score for each immune subniche. Consistent with the neighborhood analysis, the tissue-resident myeloid niches had the highest fibrosis signature score ( Figure 4 h), highlighting their role in a fibrotic tissue response. Discussion Here, we have described the landscape of immune infiltration and fibrosis in the kidneys of patients with ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN. Using high-resolution spatial transcriptomic analysis, we elucidated key features of ICI-AIN, including a strong activation of IFN-γ/STAT1 signaling, a reduction in oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells, and a heterogeneous immune cell infiltration. Based on the Tessera algorithm 19 for the identification of niches with similar transcriptional profiles, we were able to identify biologically meaningful, functional units, thereby circumventing the problems associated with cell segmentation. Some niches corresponded to histoanatomical parts of the kidney, like the glomeruli or specific segments of the tubule, allowing us to compare the gene expression within specific kidney regions. Other niche types corresponded to pathological changes, including immune cell infiltration and fibrosis. Clustering-based analyses enabled us to investigate the heterogeneity of the immune cell infiltrate in detail, highlighting how TLS-like structures, myeloid cell-dominant inflammation, and fibrotic processes happen in parallel within the ICI-AIN-damaged kidney. Analyzing the spatial expression of chemokine and/or receptor pairs enabled us to understand the mechanisms that determine the architecture of these meta-structures. Our analyses found that CD8 + T cells are associated with the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN given the limited control of ICI-ATN ( Figure 5 ). T cell infiltration appeared to play a functional role in all the immune cell niches we identified, and T cell-related genes were among the most abundant in all niches. These T cells, expressing markers of repeated activation like PD1, CTLA4, and LAG3, seemed to coordinate the recruitment and activation of other immune cells by the expression of CXCL13 (attracting B and T cells and forming TLS-like structures) and IFN-γ (inducing an inflammatory myeloid phenotype). These inflammatory myeloid cells, in turn, may have induced tissue damage by producing metalloproteases like MMP9 and by recruiting additional CXCR3-expressing inflammatory cells producing CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11. Figure 5 Schematic of the inferred pathophysiology in ICI-AIN with a focus on the role of CD8 + T cells. CD8 + T cells with transcriptional markers of tissue-residency and repeated stimulation are the main producers of IFN-γ. IFN-γ reduces oxidative phosphorylation in kidney tubules and induces a proinflammatory program in myeloid cells. These proinflammatory myeloid cells lead to tissue damage and also produce the chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11, attracting additional CXCR3 + lymphocytes, including additional CD8 + T cells. CD8 + T cells also produce CXCL13, a chemokine that attracts B cells and induces the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures in the kidney. Notably, CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN recapitulated features associated with T cells of the tumor microenvironment with transcriptional features of exhaustion and instigation of TLS structures by the production of CXCL13. 30 , 31 , 32 Plasma cells also showed increased abundance in the ICI-AIN samples, and we hypothesize that these indicate productive B-T cell interactions in these TLS-like structures. Plasma cells have also been identified in ICI-associated myocarditis; however, no antibodies against myocardial antigens were identified. 12 Although T cells in ICI-ATN samples showed a transcriptional signature typical of short-lived effector cells (expressing KLRG1 and CX3CR1 ), the CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN expressed more HOBIT ( ZNF683 ), CD103 ( ITGAE ), and CXCR6, markers of tissue-resident memory cells. 33 Interestingly, a CD8 + T cell subset with high expression of HOBIT was identified in the peripheral blood of a patient with kidney allograft rejection after ICI treatment. 34 A similar signature of ITGAE + tissue-resident T cells was recently reported in ICI-related colitis. 11 It is therefore plausible that CD8 + tissue-resident memory T cells, disinhibited by ICI treatment, are the primary cell type that initiates the inflammatory cascade observed in ICI-AIN. Our analyses also implicated niches with a high density of a tissue-resident transcription profile in the development of kidney fibrosis. This is consistent with recent reports highlighting the role of a similar population in fibrotic damage in lupus nephritis. 35 , 36 Although we reported the spatial association of these niches with fibrotic area, future research is needed to determine if these cells mediate fibrosis or protect against further damage. The immunological changes we observed may inform the selection of novel treatment targets in ICI-AIN. Currently, ICI-AIN is treated by holding or discontinuing ICIs and administering glucocorticoids, which may compromise anti-tumor immune response. 37 , 38 Drugs targeting IFN-γ and its receptors, and especially drugs such as baricitinib and ruxolitinib—which target the downstream signaling of Janus Kinase and/or STAT—may thus have greater utility in treating ICI-AIN. To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive spatial data of ICI-AKI to date; however, there were limitations. Alignment of kidney structures with spatial transcriptomic areas was poor, and high-resolution images of H&E stainings were performed on serial sections. Furthermore, kidney biopsies from patients with ICI-AIN show great heterogeneity, and the small number of samples analyzed, along with the lack of inclusion of “healthy” controls, may have limited our ability to explore key differences. Notably, medullary cell types and niches were overrepresented in the ICI-AIN samples because of higher representation of kidney medulla in ICI-AIN samples. However, we chose the ICI-ATN group as controls as they share important confounding features with the ICI-AIN group (malignant disease, cancer treatment, and unspecific kidney tissue changes caused by AKI). Additionally, the commercial Xenium 5K panel may have limited utility in providing insight into cell types within the nephron. Methods for cellular segmentation in spatial transcriptomic and proteomic analyses are still an area of active investigation; thus, transcripts of neighboring cells may spill over and dilute marker gene identification, especially in areas with challenging cell morphologies, such as the glomerulus. Current spatial transcriptomic approaches result in relatively sparse data, which can lead to biases. For example, the emphasis on CD8 + T cells in our data could, at least in part, be explained by the higher transcript density of CD8A compared with CD4 . Although we used a niche-based approach to mitigate these limitations, orthogonal approaches like single-cell transcriptomics in ICI-AIN will be needed to phenotype infiltrating immune cells at higher resolution. In summary, we used spatial transcriptomics to show that IFN-γ-producing CD8 + T cells may be implicated in the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN, and that CD8 + T cell-derived IFN-γ likely induces a proinflammatory state in myeloid cells, with increased tissue production of CXCL9, 10, and 11. Future studies with a larger number of samples will be needed to validate our findings and investigate the association of specific immune niche subsets with disease severity and/or refractoriness, treatment response, and likelihood of kidney recovery. evidence_text: Iron-catalyzed oxidative stress reveals an exposome-related ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche in BRCA1-linked renal carcinogenesis. Early cancer initiation under chronic oxidative stress requires the survival of epithelial cells that should otherwise be eliminated by regulated cell death. However, the spatial and morphological identity of such stress-adapted cells remains poorly defined. Here, we integrated Xenium single-cell spatial transcriptomics, quantitative nuclear morphometrics, mitochondrial analyses, and human cancer datasets to investigate iron-driven renal carcinogenesis in Brca1(L63X/+) rats. Ferric nitrilotriacetate exposure induced dynamic remodeling of proximal tubular epithelium, characterized by loss of homeostatic transport and mitochondrial programs, and activation of Myc, Met, Lcn2, Anxa2 and iron-handling genes. BRCA1 haploinsufficiency expanded a karyomegalic proximal tubular state associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, chromatin hyperchromasia, nuclear remodeling, and ferroptosis-resistant transcriptional features. Subclassification of karyomegalic cells identified distinct stress-adaptive populations, including a BRCA1-associated K2 state enriched for Myc/Met/Lcn2 signaling and preferentially embedded within a pro-oncogenic epithelial-stromal microenvironment. Of note, neighboring non-karyomegalic proximal tubular cells acquired related iron-handling and survival-biased programs, indicating that karyomegaly marks a broader pre-neoplastic field rather than an isolated abnormality. Human TCGA renal cancer analyses and morphometric assessment of BRCA1-mutant breast tissue further supported the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated gene modules and nuclear remodeling. These findings define a spatially organized, ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche as an early lesion in iron-driven carcinogenesis and establish quantitative nuclear morphology as a functional readout of exposome-related oxidative stress adaptation in genetically susceptible tissues. mutant) rat     n.s.   not significant     NSD   nuclear substructure density     OA_PT    oxidative stress–adaptive  proximal tubule     OCR   oxygen-consumption rate     PCA   principal component analysis     PFI   progression-free interval     PII   peripheral intensity index     PT   proximal tubule (tubular cell[s])     RCA   rolling circle amplification     RCC   renal cell carcinoma     REF   rat embryonic fibroblast     ROI   region of interest     ssGSEA   single-sample gene set enrichment analysis     ST   stromal cell(s)     STN   solid tissue normal (non-tumorous portion)     TA   tissue array     TCGA   The Cancer Genome Atlas     TEM   transmission electron microscopy     TR_PT    transient regenerative  proximal tubule     UMAP   uniform manifold approximation and projection     WSI   whole slide image (imaging)     WT   wild-type       1  Introduction  Iron is essential for life [ 1 ], yet its redox activity also drives oxidative reactions that promote mutagenesis and malignant transformation [ 2 , 3 ]. Although persistent oxidative stress is increasingly recognized as a trigger of tumor initiation, how damaged epithelial cells survive this hostile redox environment and acquire tumor-initiating potential remains poorly understood. We previously established a ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) model of Fenton reaction–driven carcinogenesis that reproducibly induces metastatic renal adenocarcinomas and enables mechanistic analysis of oxidative stress–mediated tumorigenesis [ [4] ,  [5] ,  [6] ]. However, the spatially organized molecular programs that allow a subset of injured epithelial cells to evade elimination and persist as pre-neoplastic precursors have not been defined.  Hereditary cancers account for 5–10% of human malignancies [ 7 , 8 ]. Among hereditary cancer genes,  BRCA1  and  BRCA2  are best known for their association with breast and ovarian cancers [ 9 ], but growing evidence suggests broader roles in epithelial cancer susceptibility, including renal cell carcinoma [ 10 , 11 ]. We recently established Brca1/2 haploinsufficient rat models that recapitulate key aspects of human disease [ [12] ,  [13] ,  [14] ]. Notably, Fe-NTA–induced carcinogenesis is markedly accelerated in Brca1 haploinsufficient rats and accompanied by recurrent  c-Myc  amplification and mitochondrial abnormalities during early tumorigenesis [ 15 , 16 ]. These findings raise the possibility that BRCA1 deficiency promotes the emergence of stress-adaptive epithelial states that evade ferroptotic elimination during tumor initiation.  Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics enable single-cell–resolution molecular profiling while preserving tissue architecture and histological context [ 17 ]. Here, we integrated Xenium-based spatial transcriptomics with quantitative digital nuclear morphometrics to investigate early carcinogenic processes under iron-driven oxidative stress. This approach identified a previously unrecognized ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic epithelial population associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oncogenic signaling, and iron-handling programs. Integration with human cancer datasets further suggested that related stress-adaptive programs and nuclear abnormalities may be relevant to human epithelial tumorigenesis. Together, our findings establish a spatial and morphological framework for understanding how exposome-related [ 18 ] oxidative stress intersects with hereditary susceptibility during the earliest stages of tumor initiation.    2  Materials and methods   2.1  Renal carcinogenesis model by ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA)  All the animal experiments were approved by the animal experimental committee of Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine.  Sprague-Dawley  strain male rats of wild-type (WT) and  Brca1(L63X/+ ; mutant, MUT) [ 12 ] were bred as described previously [ 15 ]. Representative kidney specimens of 1 and 3 weeks under the carcinogenesis protocol were obtained and fixed either in phosphate-buffered 10% formalin for 48 h for paraffin-embedding, or 2 % glutaraldehyde in 1 mM phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for resin-embedding.    2.2  Tissue array construction  Six formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) rat kidney samples were organized into a tissue array (TA) format to enable simultaneous Xenium processing (three samples per slide; two slides per instrument run). RNA quality was pre-verified by RNAScope in situ on the sections from all the donor blocks. After confirmation, sample area was selected and manually extracted to re-form new TA blocks with samples coring within proper size of area (∼12 mm × 24 mm). From each TA block, 5 μm sections were cut with a rotary microtome (Leica RM2135) and mounted onto  Xenium  adhesive slides (10x Genomics). Sections were dried overnight, then stored in a desiccator until processing. All cutting and mounting steps were performed with precautions to maintain tissue morphology and RNA integrity (sterile, RNase-free tools and surfaces).    2.3  Gene panel design  A custom 50-gene  Xenium In Situ  probe panel (ID:  TCMFHM ) was designed for  Rattus norvegicus  using the 10x Genomics Custom Panel Designer ( Table S1 ). Target genes were selected to represent major renal cell types and key kidney injury pathways, prioritizing established marker genes for nephron segments (proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct principal/intercalated cells), glomerular cell types (podocytes, endothelial), interstitial cells (stromal cells), immune infiltrates (inflammatory cells), and urothelium, alongside transcripts implicated in our previous differential expression array analyses [ 15 , 19 , 20 ]. Gene selection was further guided by a published rat kidney single-cell transcriptomic atlas (E-GEAD-450 [ 21 ]), retaining only genes with robust, cell type-specific expression in the reference dataset. The final panel included renal biomarkers and ferroptosis-, oncogenic/tumor suppressor-, mitochondria-associated genes relevant to renal pathophysiology [ 15 , 22 ]. Probes were tiled across exonic regions with high specificity, minimizing off-target homology and maximizing RNA accessibility; negative control and decoding control probes were included for quality control [ 23 ].    2.4  Xenium in situ workflow  FFPE tissue sections (5 μm) were processed using the Xenium FFPE in situ transcriptomics protocol (10x Genomics, v1.0; Demonstrated Protocol  CG000580 ;  Fig. 1 A). Briefly, sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, subjected to antigen retrieval and RNA exposure, and enzymatically digested under RNase-free conditions to facilitate probe penetration while preserving tissue morphology. Probe hybridization was performed at 50 °C for approximately 18 h. After stringent washes, adjacently hybridized probe pairs were ligated for 2 h at 37 °C and amplified by rolling circle amplification (RCA) for 2 h at 30 °C to generate detectable signals [ 24 ]. Tissue autofluorescence was reduced by chemical quenching, and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for visualization and segmentation. Processed slides were mounted in Xenium imaging buffer, sealed in Xenium cassettes, and stored at 4 °C in the dark until analysis.  Fig. 1   Xenium in situ enables spatially resolved single-cell atlas of the rat kidney with customized gene panel.  A,  Experimental workflow: Wild-type (WT) and  Brca1 -mutant (MUT) rats received ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) treatment and were dissected at the indicated time-points (control, 1 week, 3 weeks) to obtain kidneys. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) sections were processed on the Xenium platform. Following in-situ transcript capture and high-plex imaging, the identical sections were stained with H&E to provide histological context (Scale bars, 10 μm).  B , UMAP embedding of Xenium-profiled cells from the WT control kidney, marked by cell-type annotation derived from canonical marker genes ( Table S1 ).  C,  Dot-plot of the top markers per cell type. Circle size indicates the percentage of nuclei expressing the gene; color denotes mean of normalized expression (z-scored).  D,  WT control renal cortex: H&E image overlaid with Xenium-decoded cells colored by cell-type annotation in B (scale bar, 100 μm).                        2.4.1  Xenium analyzer instrument  Automated imaging and transcript decoding were performed on the 10x Genomics Xenium Analyzer using software v2.0.1.0. The instrument acquired high-resolution images through 15 iterative cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and signal removal. Four fluorescent channels were used per cycle, allowing each gene in the custom panel to be identified by a unique optical barcode. Images were acquired at 200 nm/pixel resolution with a 20× objective, and Z-stack images were collected at 0.75 μm intervals. Adjacent fields of view were tiled and computationally stitched using DAPI nuclear signals as fiducial landmarks to generate a registered whole-tissue image.  Transcripts were decoded by matching fluorescent puncta to the predefined barcode codebook. Only transcripts with a Q-score ≥20, corresponding to approximately 99% decoding accuracy, were retained for downstream analysis [ 23 ]. Detected transcripts were exported with XY coordinates, gene identities, and Q-scores. Negative-control probe signals accounted for <0.03% of total reads, indicating low background noise.    2.4.2  Cell segmentation and transcript assignment  Cell segmentation was performed using the Xenium onboard segmentation pipeline. DAPI images were used to identify nuclear boundaries, which were expanded isotropically by up to 15 μm or until they reached neighboring cell boundaries. This nuclear expansion method generated non-overlapping cell polygons approximating renal epithelial cell boundaries. Decoded transcripts located within each polygon were assigned to the corresponding cell, producing a cell-by-gene expression matrix for downstream single-cell spatial analysis [ 23 ].    2.4.3  Post-Xenium histology  After transcript profiling, the same tissue sections were re-stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) to correlate molecular data with tissue morphology. H&E images were acquired using a Leica Aperio AT2 slide scanner at 40× magnification and processed in QuPath 0.5.1 to generate OME-TIFF files. The H&E images were then aligned to DAPI images in Xenium Explorer, allowing transcript-defined cell types and spatial regions to be evaluated in relation to histological structures, such as glomeruli and renal tubules.     2.5  Bioinformatic analysis of spatial transcriptomics data   2.5.1  Data preprocessing and normalization  Xenium outputs (six rat kidney FFPE tissue samples: WT_CT, MUT_CT, WT_Fe1w, MUT_Fe1w, WT_Fe3w, MUT_Fe3w) were loaded into R (version 4.4.1) and converted to a Seurat object using Seurat v5.0.1. All data normalization was performed by SCTransform to stabilize variance transformation and to regress out sequencing-depth effects. This yielded log-normalized count data (stored in Seurat “SCT” assay) for each sample, mitigating technical variability while preserving biological variation. Low-quality cells (e.g. with extremely low transcript counts) were minimal due to Xenium's preprocessing and only cells with nCount_Xenium >0 were retained.    2.5.2  Data integration and clustering  Following normalization, the unified object containing data from six samples was processed for joint analysis. We re-ran SCTransform (merged), PCA (all genes; 30 PCs), FindNeighbors (dims 1–30), FindClusters (resolution 2.0), and UMAP (PCA), which yielded multiple clusters with distinct transcriptional signatures. Mixing across samples in PCA/UMAP was inspected to verify minimal batch effects. Clusters were manually annotated to kidney lineages (proximal tubule, stromal, endothelial, loop of Henle, collecting duct principal/intercalated, podocyte, inflammatory, proximal-like) based on canonical markers [ 21 ] and spatial context provided by Xenium Explorer. For focused analyses, we subset proximal_tubules and stromal_cells contents and re-ran the same pipeline on (i) the merged dataset to confirm lineage assignments and (ii) each compartment separately to resolve fine subclusters (pt_n; st_n) for downstream analyses.    2.5.3  Pathological score maps  Proximal-tubule clusters were defined into four pathology groups by expressional signatures and tubular morphology: normal_tubules (PT_1,2,5,6,10,11), acute_injured (PT_8), subacute_injured (PT_0,3,4,7), and dying_tubules (PT_9). Using Seurat v5.0.1 we set group identities and performed one-vs-rest DE per group with FindMarkers (two-sided Wilcoxon; min.pct = 0.2, logfc.threshold = 0.25, only.pos = TRUE). The top 10 genes by avg_log2FC per group were used for visualization (group-wise AverageExpression heatmap, z-scored by gene). For quantitative per-cell scores, we computed module scores with AddModuleScore on the available marker genes for each group (requiring ≥5 genes), using nbin = 3 and ctrl = 10 to ensure robust background control on the limited panel. Scores were then row-matched by cell_ID and merged into the Giotto (v4.2.0) object's cell_metadata for downstream spatial mapping. All plotting of score maps used fixed global min–max limits per score and unified diverging palettes to enable cross-sample comparison.    2.5.4  Morphological-transcriptomics analysis of nuclei  Nuclear polygons from Xenium segmentation (“nucleus_boundaries.csv.gz”) were imported into R (sf v1.0.19; tidyverse v2.0.0) to compute per-nucleus morphometrics: nuclear area, eccentricity (elongation, 0–1), circularity (4π·area/perimeter 2 ), compactness, convexity, solidity (area/convex hull area) and perimeter/area ratio (boundary irregularity). Polygons were linked to the same cell barcodes used in Seurat; analyses were restricted to proximal tubule cells with expression taken from the SCT assay.  For each gene–feature pair, we fit single-cell linear models per FOV (WT_Fe3w: FOV_3; MUT_Fe3w: FOV_6) with the morphology feature z-scored and technical covariates (library size, detected features) included; slopes (β) and two-sided  P  values were recorded and FDR-adjusted within FOV (Benjamini–Hochberg). As robustness checks, we computed Spearman correlations and ran elastic net models (glmnet) to assess whether multiple features jointly predict expression; a non-zero coefficient denoted feature selection.  To obtain genotype-robust effects, per-FOV slopes were combined by sample-size–weighted averaging (pooled β), and per-FOV  P  values were combined by Stouffer's method (weights ∝ √n), followed by FDR across all pairs. For each gene we derived a “consensus rank” integrating pooled β, pooled FDR, and elastic-net selection.  To identify coordinated programs, each gene was represented by its vector of pooled β across morphology features. Cosine similarity was computed between genes; pairs with similarity ≥0.6 were connected and clustered by Louvain community detection to define morphology-linked gene modules.    2.5.5  Quantification of nuclear phenotypes and integration with transcriptomics  For fields of view (FOVs) from WT_Fe3w (FOV3) and MUT_Fe3w (FOV6), nuclei were segmented using Cellpose (v2.3.2; pretrained nuclei model) [ 37 ]. Three per-cell nuclear morphological readouts were derived from the hematoxylin channel (skimage.color.rgb2hed) within each nuclear mask: (i) hematoxylin optical density (HOD), mean channel intensity following Gaussian smoothing (σ = 0.5 μm); (ii) nuclear substructure density (NSD), the count of intranuclear hematoxylin-dense foci, detected after within-nucleus 2nd-98th percentile normalization, Otsu thresholding, and filtration by area (0.3–6.0 μm 2 ) and circularity (4πA/P 2  ≥ 0.40), expressed per 100 μm 2  of nuclear area; and (iii) peripheral intensity index (PII), (mean        H  O  D   periphery      − mean        H  O  D   interior     )/section-median HOD, where peripheral (distance ≤ s) and interior (distance > s) zones were defined from a Euclidean distance transform of the nuclear boundary at shell thicknesses  s  ∈ (0.5, 1.0, 1.5) μm ( Fig. S4C ); section-median HOD was estimated once per FOV from a random sample of ∼2000 nuclei.  Cellpose-segmented nuclei were assigned Xenium cell identity via two-stage spatial registration. First, an existing QuPath-to-Xenium cell correspondence (established by manual landmark selection and iterative refinement) provided position anchors for an affine transform between the FOV image and Xenium coordinate spaces. Second, true nuclear centroids (QuPath nucleus geometry) were matched to the affine-registered Cellpose nuclei by reciprocal nearest-neighbor matching within the shared coordinate space, at the tightest tolerance (0.5–5 μm ladder) retaining ≥90% of the maximum achievable match count. PT filtering was performed after registration to avoid selection bias. Registration accuracy was confirmed by comparing QuPath's measurements (HOD;  Fig. S4A ) against Cellpose/scikit-image values.    2.5.6  Gene–morphometry association models (HOD/NSD/PII)  For each gene     g     and within a condition (WT_Fe3w; MUT_Fe3w) independently, a single-cell ordinary least-squares model was fitted:     Y  i   =  α  +   β  g   ·   X   i  g    +  γ   A  i   +   ϵ  i     where      Y  i      is the nuclear morphometric readout for cell     i     (HOD; NSD;       P  I  I   s     ),      X   i  g       is the log 1 p-normalized Xenium transcript count for gene     g     in cell     i    , and      A  i      is Cellpose-measured nuclear area (μm 2 ). Two-sided Wald p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons across 50 genes within each condition (Benjamini–Hochberg, FDR <0.05). Cross-condition concordance was assessed by Pearson correlation and sign agreement of per-gene      β  ˆ      between FOVs. Estimates were pooled by fixed-effects inverse-variance weighting:      β  ˆ    F  E    =     ∑  k    w  k     β  ˆ   k      ∑  k    w  k     ,   w  k   =  S   E  k   −  2      with pooled Wald z-statistics BH-FDR corrected across all 50 genes. Models were implemented in Python (statsmodels v0.14; scipy).    2.5.7  Karyomegaly sub-stratification and peri-karyomegaly analysis  PT cells from merged Xenium dataset were defined as karyomegalic (enlarged) if nuclear area > mean+2SD within the PT cell population, and elongated if major/minor axis ratio >2. SCTransform-normalized RNA counts from karyomegalic cells were stored as a SCTx assay. Morphological features processed from nuclear polygons were stored as a MORPH assay and reduced by PCA.  Karyomegalic PTs were then reclustered by a weighted nearest-neighbor (WNN) model that integrates RNA and morphology: SCTx PCA (dims 1–30) and a PCA of z-scored morphology (dims 1–6) were combined with FindMultiModalNeighbors (modality weights recorded as SCTx.weight/MORPH.weight), followed by UMAP on the weighted graph and Louvain communities on wsnn; we grid-searched morphology PCs (2-4, 6) × resolution (0.2, 0.3) and selected the setting with the highest mean silhouette in the WNN UMAP, followed by further resolution tuning, yielding the final result (K0–K5, resolution 0.15). Gene markers were computed using Seurat FindAllMarkers (logistic regression with covariates sample, fov_num, nCount_SCTx). Morphology tiles report per-feature means with significance from two-sided linear models (BH-FDR <0.05).  Spatial context was obtained by overlaying subcluster labels onto H&E in Xenium Explorer (Fe-NTA, 3-week). For peri-karyomegalic analyses, each karyomegalic PT served as a center; PT neighbors within 30 μm were compared with PTs >30 μm away, and hallmark expression visualized as z-scored heatmaps/dot plots (Wilcoxon, BH-FDR where indicated).    2.5.8  Neighborhood composition and microenvironment analysis  Cell centroids (centroid_x, centroid_y) and annotations from the Seurat metadata were filtered to proximal_tubules and stromal_cells, and used for point map plotting and neighbor-associated computations. Independently for each sample, the number of stromal neighbors within a 30 μm Euclidean radius was recorded for each PT cell, by a KD-tree constructed over stromal cell centroids (FNN v1.1.4.1, R; k ≤ 500). Group differences were assessed by Kruskal–Wallis test; pairwise post-hoc comparisons used Dunn's test with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction (rstatix v0.7.3, R). Beyond cell-intrinsic analysis, we modeled proximal-tubule/stromal spatial organization with Giotto (v4.2.0; Python backend) [ 25 ]. For each field, we constructed a radius-based neighbor graph (30 μm) to capture tubulointerstitial contacts in renal tissue [ 26 ]. Community detection on this neighborhood graph using the Leiden algorithm (findNetworkCommunities) yielded microenvironment (ME) clusters, i.e., spatially coherent neighborhoods that may contain mixed PT (pt_n) and stromal (st_n) subtypes. We quantified the cell-type composition and contact enrichment for each ME cluster (normalized by cell abundance). ME prevalences were compared across the six samples to assess genotype/treatment effects. ME labels were overlaid on tissue images in Xenium Explorer to verify anatomic plausibility.  To test whether ME states were independent of karyomegalic clusters, we constructed a WNN-karyomegalic × ME contingency table and applied a Pearson χ 2  test of independence (chisq.test) Tiles in the heatmap display standardized Pearson residuals (Haberman adjustment, chis$stdres): positive (green) indicates over-representation; negative (red) indicates under-representation. Significance stars denote: ∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  1.96    , ∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  2.58    , and ∗∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  3.00    . Global association was summarized by Cramér's     V  =     χ  2   /   (   N   [   min  ⁡   (   r  ,  c   )   −  1   ]    )       ; extremely small P values are reported as thresholds (e.g.,     p  <  2.2  ×   10   −  16      ).    2.5.9  Data visualization  All data visualization was performed in R (v4.4.1), using ggplot2 and plotters bundled with Seurat unless noted otherwise. Low-dimensional embeddings (UMAP) were rendered with DimPlot and annotated by cluster, sample, or FOV; single-gene summaries used VlnPlot or Seurat DotPlot. Heatmaps were produced with ComplexHeatmap for clustered expression/annotation panels and pheatmap for compact correlation/residual matrices. Panel assembly used patchwork/cowplot with harmonized color palettes, fixed aspect ratios for spatial panels, and consistent legends/scales. Multi-panel gene maps ( Fig. 2 C) and pathology-score maps ( Fig. 3 E) were generated in Giotto and exported in R. Xenium Explorer was used only to overlay labels on H&E/DAPI micrographs. Differential expression (DE) used Seurat FindMarkers/FindAllMarkers on SCT-normalized data with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Genes were eligible if detected in ≥5% of cells in either group; we report avg_log2FC (positive = higher in the first group), pct_in/pct_out, and adjusted P. Multiple testing was controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg; genes with FDR <0.05 and log 2 FC ≥ 0.25 were considered significant. Random subsampling (set.seed 42) was applied only to downsample points for visualization and was never applied in statistical testing. Box-and-violin plots display median and inter-quartile range; error bars represent 95% confidence intervals unless specified. Because the Xenium dataset included one representative specimen per genotype/treatment condition, cell-level statistics were interpreted as discovery-level measures of spatial association or enrichment rather than animal-level biological replication; key conclusions were supported by prior Fe-NTA data, mitochondrial TEM/REF analyses, and TCGA-based human validation.    2.5.11  Code availability No new algorithms were developed for this manuscript. All code created for analysis is available from the authors upon request.  Mitochondrial cristae morphometry analysis  Transmission electron microscopic images were acquired on a JEM-1400PLUS (JEOL; Tokyo, Japan). Images were analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ (v1.54p). After pixel calibration, individual mitochondria were manually outlined as ROIs with area (μm 2 ) recorded. Within each ROI, cristae ridges were segmented using Trainable Weka Segmentation (Fiji) to obtain a probability map for cristae vs. matrix. High-confidence pixels were thresholded and processed with Ridge Detection to obtain ridge centerlines, followed by Skeletonize (2D/3D) and Analyze Skeleton to quantify branch geometry. Derived per-mitochondrion metrics were: Total cristae length (μm) = Σ branch lengths;  Mean branch length (μm) = Σ branch lengths / number of branches;  Cristae length density (μm/μm 2 ) = total cristae length / mitochondrial area.   Metrics were exported as CVS files and plotted in R.    2.7  Immunoblotting  Kidney cortex lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer, resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred by standard methods. Primary antibodies included: anti-FTMT (ab124889, Abcam), anti-Mfrn1 (PA5-26720, Invitrogen), anti-Mfrn2 (PA5-42498, Invitrogen); anti-ACTB (AC-15, Sigma) served as loading control. Bands were quantified in ImageJ, normalized to ACTB, and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test; significance thresholds: ∗ P  < 0.05, ∗∗ P  < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P  < 0.001; n.s., not significant).    2.8  Primary rat embryonic fibroblasts (REFs) and treatments  REFs were derived from E13–15 embryos by standard protocols [ 28 ]. Genotypes and sex were determined by PCR [ 15 , 29 ]. Male-derived WT and Brca1-MUT REFs were maintained in DMEM (043-30085, Wako, Osaka, Japan) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Biowest; Nuaillé, France) and Mito + Serum Extender (355006, Corning, USA). REFs were immortalized via lentiviral transduction of SV40 (Addgene#22298) packaged with pspAX2 (#12260) and VSV-G (#14888). For oxidative stress, cells were treated with Fe-NTA (500 μM, 6 h) prior to fixation.    2.9  Immunofluorescence (confocal)  Cells were fixed, permeabilized and stained with anti-TOM20 (11802-1-AP, Proteintech) and anti-γ-H2AX (05-636, Sigma-Aldrich); nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. A Zeiss confocal microscope (LSM880, Carl Zeiss) was applied for image acquisition.    2.10  Mitochondrial respiration  Oxygen consumption (OCR) and extracellular acidification (ECAR) were measured on a Seahorse XFe24 Analyzer (Agilent) following manufacture's instructions. Briefly, REFs were seeded (6 × 10 4 /well) in Seahorse XF DMEM (103575-100) supplemented with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine (103577/8/9-100) on a Seahorse XFe24 plate and incubated overnight. The XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (103015-100) was run with sequential injections of oligomycin 1.5 μM, FCCP 1 μM, and rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 μM. Cell count was quantified using BioTek Cytation 5 and Keyence BZ-X800 for normalization. Data were processed per manufacturer's instructions and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test with significance shown in  Fig. 8 E ).    2.11  TCGA transcriptomic cohorts  To evaluate the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated transcriptional programs identified in our experimental model, we analyzed data obtained from the TCGA Pan-Cancer Clinical Data Resource, for TCGA-KIRC as the primary validation cohort, and additional tumor types for exploratory analyses, including TCGA-BRCA, TCGA-COAD, TCGA-LIHC, TCGA-LUAD, and TCGA-LUSC [ 30 ].  RNA-seq data were retrieved via TCGAbiolinks v2.32.0 [ 31 ] from the NCI GDC. Tumor-adjacent solid tissue normal (STN) samples were used for the primary analyses, whereas primary tumor samples were evaluated separately for independent validation. Raw counts were normalized by the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method using edgeR v4.2.2 [ 32 ] and converted to log 2 -counts per million (log 2 -CPM; prior count = 1). For duplicate gene entries, the isoform with the highest mean expression was retained.   2.11.1  Karyomegalic module definition and scoring  Four gene modules were evaluated (Fig. S7A). Three gene modules were defined based on findings from our Xenium spatial transcriptomics data. Module activity was quantified by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) using GSVA v1.52.3 [ 33 ], computed independently within each tissue compartment (STN or tumor). Only modules with at least three genes present in the expression matrix were retained. Patient-level scores were derived as mean across available samples.    2.11.2  Survival analysis  Clinical annotations, including progression-free interval (PFI) and overall survival (OS), were obtained from curated TCGA clinical datasets. For each module, patients were stratified into high- and low-score groups using the cohort-specific median module score as the cutoff. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated using the survival and survminer packages.  Associations between module activity and clinical outcome were evaluated using log-rank tests and univariable Cox proportional hazards models. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated from Cox models. Analyses were performed separately for PFI and OS endpoints. Cohorts with fewer than five outcome events or insufficient matched samples were excluded from survival testing.  A tiered strategy was used for Multiple-testing correction. We designated TCGA-KIRC as the confirmatory cohort and analyzed non-renal cancer cohorts in an exploratory manner. Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was therefore performed separately within confirmatory and exploratory tiers. Statistical significance was assessed primarily using the tier-specific FDR-adjusted results.    2.11.3  BRCA1 mutation carrier and control definition  BRCA1 germline carriers were defined as described [ 34 ]. Non-carrier controls were identified by a two-tiered exclusion strategy requiring availability of diagnostic WSIs and absence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, RAD51C, RAD51D, BARD1, and NBN. Controls were further selected by two-stage propensity score matching to control for clinical covariates [ 35 ] .  The final cohort comprised 20 BRCA1 germline carriers and 63 matched non-carrier controls (76.2% ductal, 4.8% lobular, 19.0% other histological subtypes).    2.11.4  Histopathological image analysis  Diagnostic whole slide images (WSIs) for TCGA-BRCA were obtained from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (GDC). Germline variant data were accessed from the TCGA PanCanAtlas Germline dataset [ 34 ] under controlled GDC access (dbGaP: phs000178), in compliance with the TCGA data use agreement.  Regions of interest (ROIs) containing well-formed ductal tubules were manually annotated in ductal carcinoma WSIs from both groups using QuPath v0.4 [ 36 ] (15 controls, 7 carriers; ROI count was limited by preserved adjacent normal portions). Nucleus segmentation was performed using Cellpose v2.3.2 [ 37 ], and morphological features were extracted using scikit-image. A post-hoc quality filter was applied to remove spurious detections. Nucleus-level analyses are presented as exploratory findings; patient-level analyses constitute the primary statistical inference.      3  Results   3.1  Xenium in situ on early stages of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis  To identify early alterations during iron-driven renal carcinogenesis, we analyzed kidneys from wild-type (WT) and  Brca1  mutant ( L63X/+ ; MUT) rats subjected to Fe-NTA administration, as previously described [ 15 ]. Because rat-compatible spatial transcriptomic panels remain limited, we designed a custom 50-gene Xenium panel covering renal structural markers from single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets [ 21 ], together with genes related to iron metabolism, mitochondrial function, and tumorigenesis based on our previous studies [ 5 , 38 ].  Six kidney samples representing control, 1-week, and 3-week Fe-NTA exposure in WT and MUT rats were analyzed across two Xenium slides. DAPI-based segmentation captured approximately 324,765–531,476 cells per sample, with median transcript detection of 62–104 transcripts per cell ( Fig. 1 A). Post-Xenium H&E staining preserved tissue morphology and enabled direct integration of spatial transcriptomics with histopathology ( Fig. 1 A–D). Seurat-based clustering identified 53 cellular clusters, which were annotated into 10 major renal cell categories based on marker expression and histological context ( Fig. 1 B and C;  Fig. S1A and B ). Molecular annotations closely matched H&E-defined structures, supporting robust cell-type assignment even with a focused gene panel ( Fig. 1 D). Cluster composition varied across genotype and treatment conditions, with prominent changes in proximal tubules and stromal cells ( Fig. S1C ), indicating early remodeling of epithelial and interstitial compartments during Fe-NTA-induced carcinogenesis.    3.2  Characterization of key-gene signatures in early renal carcinogenesis  We next focused on transcriptional remodeling of proximal tubular cells (PTs), the principal target of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis. Refined clustering of PT and stromal compartments improved resolution of treatment- and genotype-associated cell states ( Fig. S2A and B ). Single-cell expression analysis revealed reciprocal regulation of homeostatic and injury-associated genes in PTs ( Fig. 2 A). In control kidneys, PTs highly expressed renal function and mitochondrial metabolism genes, hereafter referred to as “friend key-genes,” including  Lrp2, Pink1,  and  Amacr . In contrast, Fe-NTA exposure induced “foe key-genes” associated with injury and tumorigenesis, including  Myc, Met, Lcn2 , and  Anxa2 , with concomitant reduction of homeostatic markers.  Several foe key-genes were induced as early as 1 week after Fe-NTA exposure in both genotypes ( Fig. 2 A). Although  Met, Anxa2, Lcn2, Sfxn3 , and  Klf4  showed partial reduction by 3 weeks,  Myc  and  Slc22a17  remained elevated or further increased. At 3 weeks, MUT PTs showed stronger expression of foe markers than WT, whereas  Lrp2  and  Amacr  were more strongly reduced, indicating genotype-dependent epithelial remodeling under oxidative stress. Spatial mapping with Giotto confirmed that friend key-genes were enriched in intact tubular segments, whereas foe key-genes localized to histologically abnormal regions with tubular dilation, disruption, or loss of recognizable tubular organization ( Fig. 2 C).  Because karyomegalic PTs are a characteristic lesion in Fe-NTA-treated kidneys [ 39 , 40 ], we quantified nuclear morphology using Xenium-derived nuclear polygons ( Fig. 2 B). Fe-NTA exposure was associated with nuclear enlargement, reduced compactness and circularity, and increased eccentricity. WT karyomegalic cells had larger nuclei than MUT cells under comparable treatment conditions ( Fig. S5A ). These data indicate that nuclear remodeling accompanies early Fe-NTA-induced epithelial injury and is modified by Brca1 haploinsufficiency.    3.3  Dynamics of diverse PT subtypes in early renal carcinogenesis  To resolve PT dynamics during early carcinogenesis, we reclustered PTs and identified 11 subtypes ( Fig. 3 A and B). Homeostatic PT clusters 1, 2, 5, 6, 10, and 12 predominated in control kidneys and expressed renal functional and mitochondrial genes. In contrast, clusters 0, 3, 4, 7, 8, and 9 emerged after Fe-NTA exposure and showed increased injury-, repair-, or foe key-gene expression with reduced homeostatic programs. Genotype-specific differences became evident after Fe-NTA exposure: WT kidneys showed transient loss of normal tubular states at 1 week with partial recovery by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed expansion of injured clusters, particularly clusters 4 and 7.  The PT subtypes represented distinct biological states ( Fig. 3 B). Oxidative Stress–Adaptive PTs (cluster 0; OA_PT) expressed antioxidant and metabolic genes such as  Cubn, Slc40a1, Lrp2, Slc27a2 , and  Gpx4 , together with moderate  Myc  and  Met  expression. DNA Damage–Response PTs (cluster 3; DR_PT) expressed repair and regenerative markers including  Mki67, Rad51, Bard1 , and  Bap1 . Maladaptive Repair PTs (clusters 4 and 7; MR_PT) expressed  Lcn2, Slc22a17 , and other foe key-genes, with cluster 4 retaining more friend key-gene expression than cluster 7. Transient Regenerative PTs (cluster 8; TR_PT) expressed proliferation and DNA repair markers, whereas Ferroptotic PTs (cluster 9; Fer_PT) were often isolated necrotic or pyknotic cells within otherwise preserved tubules, as confirmed by Xenium Explorer alignment with H&E images ( Fig. S3A ).  Spatially, DR_PT localized mainly near the cortex–medulla boundary in WT kidneys at 1 week but was less evident in MUT kidneys ( Fig. 3 C). MR_PT populations frequently co-localized within MUT tubules, whereas WT tubules showed greater admixture of homeostatic, oxidative stress–adaptive, and transient regenerative states. Stromal reclustering further identified 13 stromal subtypes with genotype- and treatment-dependent composition ( Fig. 3 D). After 3 weeks of Fe-NTA, MUT kidneys showed expansion of stromal states enriched for regenerative, injury-response, iron-handling, matrix-remodeling, and macrophage-recruiting signatures, including ST_1, ST_3, ST_5/8, ST_6, and ST_9.  To summarize PT status spatially, we generated pathology-informed module scores ( Fig. S3B–D ). Spatial score maps showed that normal tubular scores declined after 1 week of Fe-NTA exposure and partially recovered in WT kidneys by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed more persistent dysfunction ( Fig. 3 E). Interestingly, scores representing renal injury and cell death (acute/subacute injured score; dying tubules score) displayed inverse spatial patterns to normal tubules score at 1-week Fe-NTA treatment, with reduced acute injured score at 3-week Fe-NTA treatment, marking the progression of homeostatic PT clusters toward subacute injury and the initiation of cellular adaptations linked to ferroptosis resistance and potential oncogenic transformation.    3.4  Nuclear morphometrics reflect transcriptional behaviors in pathological/genotype-dependent patterns  We next asked whether nuclear morphology captures transcriptional states at single-cell resolution. Morphological features derived from Xenium polygons included nuclear area, eccentricity, circularity, compactness, convexity, and solidity ( Fig. 4 A). Gene–morphology associations were quantified using covariate-adjusted linear models with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction.
