However, these datasets are prone to signal saturation from highly expressed genes, which can obscure biologically meaningful signals from low‐abundance transcripts [ 4 ]. To address this limitation, we applied STWave to capture multi‐scale gene expression patterns in ultra‐large ST datasets and to amplify signals that exhibit intrinsic spatial structure.  We evaluated STWave on a Xenium human breast cancer dataset comprising 1 67 780 spots and 313 genes [ 4 ], and compared its performance with HERGAST [ 20 ], STAGATE, and PCA. Specifically, STWave outperformed all competing methods in terms of Adjusted Rand Index (ARI: 0.546) and Homogeneity Score (HS: 0.656), demonstrating a clear advantage in discriminating closely related cell types. Although HERGAST achieved a marginally higher Normalized Mutual Information (0.580 versus 0.547), STWave generated clusters with superior histological concordance and more faithful boundary delineation. By contrast, STAGATE exhibited pronounced oversmoothing and cluster merging in this dataset, leading to the loss of biologically meaningful local structures. In addition, STAGATE produced fragmented and irregular domain boundaries across tissue regions, thereby reducing overall spatial coherence ( Figure   4a,b ). To keep the main figure readable and highlight comparisons with PCA as a non‐spatial baseline and STAGATE as a spatial baseline, the complete HERGAST spatial visualization is provided in Figure  S9 , and the quantitative comparison is summarized in Figure  S12 . To verify that STWave enhances biologically meaningful signals in reconstructed expression, we examined the spatial patterns of key breast cancer markers in both the raw and reconstructed data, including     C  D  H  1    ,     C  E  A  C  A  M  6    ,     E  P  C  A  M    , and     E  R  B  B  2     (Figure  4c ; extended feature plots across multiple baselines are shown in Figures  S10  and  S11 ). The reconstructed expression patterns more clearly delineated a triple‐positive region, consistent with prior observations [ 4 ]. This observation was further supported by a quantitative assessment using the region‐specific relative marker signal gain (RSG), defined in Equations ( S14 )–( S18 ) as the ratio of the mean min–max‐normalized marker signal in the reconstructed map to that in the raw map within the corresponding H&E‐defined region. Across the selected marker‐region pairs in the Xenium human breast cancer dataset, the reconstructed maps showed consistently increased relative normalized marker signals, with RSG values ranging from 2.08   ×    to 4.42   ×    (Table  S15 ). These results indicate that STWave increases region‐specific relative marker signal intensity while avoiding interpretation as an absolute expression fold change. At the individual‐slice level, we next analyzed slice #151672, which exhibits well‐defined cortical layers and white matter (Figure  6a ). STWave achieved an adjusted rand index (ARI) of 0.796 and a normalized mutual information (NMI) of 0.678, accurately delineating all laminar boundaries in close agreement with manual annotations (Figure  6c  and Tables  S8  and  S9 ). By contrast, baseline methods exhibited distinct topological failure modes. Although BayesSpace achieved a relatively high normalized mutual information (NMI: 0.702), it failed to resolve the biological boundary between Layers 4 and 5 and erroneously subdivided Layer 6 into two domains. Similarly, MuCoST, STAGATE, SEDR, and DeepGFT misclassified Layer 3 by fragmenting it into discontinuous regions. Further validation using UMAP and PAGA analyses confirmed that STWave can capture continuous biological trajectories underlying tissue organization. The learned embeddings distinctly separated layer‐specific spots while preserving smooth transitions that recapitulate the physical continuity of the tissue. In contrast, methods such as conST failed to recover this connectivity or to accurately resolve laminar boundaries. This improved performance is likely attributable to the integration of a discrete wavelet transform with a graph attention autoencoder, which enhances layer‐specific molecular signals while attenuating noise (Figure  6d,f  and Figures  S21  and  S22 ).     3  Conclusion  STWave represents a scalable computational paradigm designed to bridge the gap between the massive data volumes of the     μ  ST     era and constrained hardware resources. As ST technologies advance toward subcellular resolution, the exponential increase in spot numbers poses a substantial memory barrier for existing analytical tools. Our framework addresses this challenge by introducing a unified pipeline tailored for ultra‐large ST datasets. It enables routine analysis of hundreds of thousands of spots on standard computing platforms without compromising biological resolution. By formulating spatial domain identification as a joint problem of computational efficiency and signal enhancement, STWave offers a robust solution for decoding tissue heterogeneity at microscopic scales.  The effectiveness of STWave arises from two core mechanisms that jointly balance scalability and accuracy. First, the partition‐and‐sample strategy addresses the memory bottleneck by enabling patch‐based computation during both training and inference. Second, the integration of a discrete wavelet transform mitigates extreme sparsity and noise characteristic of subcellular‐resolution data. Specifically, approximation coefficients capture global tissue patterns, whereas detail coefficients preserve sharp spatial boundaries. The dual‐domain reconstruction loss further encourages the model to learn representations that are consistent across the wavelet and gene‐expression domains, effectively suppressing technical noise while retaining weak but biologically meaningful signals.  Extensive validation across diverse ST platforms underscores STWave's ability to uncover biologically meaningful patterns that are overlooked by existing approaches. Beyond improvements in standard quantitative metrics, STWave consistently resolved subtle yet clinically relevant structures. For example, in colorectal cancer, it delineated the spatial niche of     S  P  P   1  +      tumor‐associated macrophages and pro‐tumor inflammatory regions enriched for     C  X  C  L  8    . In mouse embryonic development, STWave uniquely identified a dorsal forebrain subregion defined by     F  o  x  g  1    , in close agreement with established histological knowledge. Moreover, STWave outperformed 17 baselines on the Visium DLPFC benchmark, demonstrating superior resolution of fine‐grained cortical layers. These results indicate that the combination of multi‐scale modeling and efficient partitioning enables robust generalization across diverse biological contexts and ST technologies.  Despite these advantages, several limitations suggest directions for future improvement. Fixed‐size patching may disrupt continuous spatial structures at boundaries, which could be alleviated by adaptive or overlapping strategies. To quantify this effect, boundary and interior regions were compared on the Xenium human breast cancer dataset under different boundary ranges. The boundary‐region ARI and NMI remained comparable to the corresponding interior‐region values, suggesting that the patch‐based strategy did not introduce substantial performance degradation at patch boundaries in this dataset (Table  S14 ). In addition, representing gene expression as a 1D sequence does not fully capture gene‐gene regulatory relationships; graph‐based embeddings or order‐invariant transforms may provide more expressive alternatives. Finally, extending STWave from two‐dimensional (2D) sections to three‐dimensional (3D) reconstruction or multi‐modal integration would further enhance its applicability.    4  Experimental Section   4.1  Data Description  We evaluated STWave on a collection of ST datasets spanning multiple technologies and spatial resolutions. The study encompasses five platforms: 10x Genomics Visium HD, 10x Genomics Xenium, NanoString CosMx SMI, BGI Stereo‐seq, and 10x Genomics Visium. Among these, Visium HD achieves near‐cellular resolution with     2  ×  2   μ  m     features across a     6.5   mm  ×  6.5   mm     tissue area, with measurements that can be aggregated into coarser spatial spots ranging from     8     to     16   μ  m    . Xenium is an imaging‐based in situ platform that provides single‐cell to subcellular resolution using ready‐to‐use panels of 5000 genes, with options for small add‐ons or fully custom designs. NanoString CosMx SMI similarly achieves single‐cell to subcellular resolution and supports RNA panels targeting about 6000 genes in both FFPE and fresh‐frozen tissues. Stereo‐seq employs DNA nanoball–patterned arrays on flexible chip formats, enabling spatial binning from subcellular to multicellular scales. In contrast, the Visium platform profiles transcriptomes using 55     μ  m     circular spots across a     6.5   mm  ×  6.5   mm     capture area, providing multicellular resolution with one to ten cells per spot. Collectively, these platforms span spatial resolutions from multicellular to subcellular scales, motivating the development of methods that preserve fine‐grained biological detail while maintaining computational efficiency.  To evaluate the accuracy of spatial domain identification, we benchmarked STWave on a human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) dataset comprising 12 tissue slices from three donors, with each capture area containing about 4000 spots and 33 538 genes. To assess performance at single‐cell and subcellular resolutions, we analyzed a diverse array of high‐resolution ST datasets: a Visium HD human colorectal cancer slice (P2) containing 5 45 913 spots and 18 085 genes; two Xenium datasets, including a human breast cancer dataset featuring 1 67 780 spots across 313 genes and a human kidney cancer dataset containing 56 510 spots across 377 genes; and a CosMx SMI lung cancer dataset consisting of 87 589 spots and 960 genes. The longitudinal Stereo‐seq mouse embryo series (stages E13.5–E16.5) was further utilized, with the E16.5 sample totaling 1 55 741 spots and 28 579 genes. To test high‐resolution scalability under resource‐constrained environments, we generated a series of simulated datasets from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, spanning     5  ×   10  3      to     6.4  ×   10  5      spots. This comprehensive collection covers a continuous spectrum from small‐scale to ultra‐large‐scale data. Collectively, these benchmarks evaluate whether STWave preserves spatial fidelity and maintains manageable resource consumption as data volume increases, while highlighting where baseline methods succumb to oversmoothing of fine structures, boundary fragmentation, or computational failure.    4.2  Data Preprocessing  Gene expression data were processed using Scanpy. For datasets containing at least 3000 genes, highly variable genes were identified from the raw counts using the Seurat v3 method, and the top 3000 highly variable genes were retained. The resulting expression matrix was then normalized on a per‐spot basis and log‐transformed. For datasets with fewer than 3000 genes, all genes were retained before normalization and log transformation, as in the Xenium human breast cancer and CosMx SMI human lung cancer datasets.    4.3  Spatial Neighbor Graph Construction  We construct a spatial graph based on the Euclidean distances between spot coordinates. Spatial relationships are encoded as an undirected    k   ‐nearest‐neighbor graph, denoted      G  spatial   =   (   V  spatial   ,   E  spatial   )     , where     V  spatial     denotes the set of spots and     E  spatial     denotes the set of undirected edges connecting neighboring spots. The adjacency matrix is denoted      A  spatial   ∈    {  0  ,  1  }    n  ×  n      , where    n    is the number of spots. For vertices    i    and    j   , we set      a  spatial   i  j    =  1     if    j    belongs to the set of    k    nearest neighbors of    i   , and      a  spatial   i  j    =  0     otherwise. Each spot is connected to its    k    nearest neighbors, and the resulting graph is treated as undirected. In our experiments, we set     k  =  8     for simulated data, Visium HD, Xenium, and Stereo‐seq datasets, and     k  =  6     for standard 10x Visium datasets.  Based on the constructed spatial graph, STWave prunes edges that are unlikely to convey meaningful local information. We first embed the gene expression matrix using PCA and obtain an initial partition of spots via the Louvain algorithm. Edge pruning is then performed in two stages. In the first stage, edges connecting spots assigned to different clusters are removed to prevent premature information propagation across heterogeneous regions. In the second stage, spurious long‐range connections are eliminated using distance‐based outlier detection with an Isolation Forest [ 46 ]. Specifically, edges with unusually large Euclidean lengths (e.g., exceeding the global mean plus one standard deviation) are flagged and removed. The resulting pruned graph is denoted      G  pruned   =   (   V  pruned   ,   E  pruned   )     .    4.4  Wavelet Representation of Gene Expression  ST data are high‐dimensional and sparse, characterized by pronounced zero inflation, technical noise, multi‐scale texture, and fragile tissue boundaries. These properties often lead to over‐smoothing, attenuation of weak biological signals, and unstable alignment across tissue sections. To disentangle background variation from edge information across multiple scales, we represent the expression profile of each spot as a 1D discrete signal ordered by gene index and apply a 1D discrete wavelet transform [ 47 ]. This 1D representation is used as a computationally efficient multi‐scale feature transform rather than as an explicit model of gene regulatory interactions. To assess whether the imposed gene order affects downstream performance, randomized gene‐order experiments were conducted on the DLPFC dataset, where ARI and NMI remained stable across five random orders (Figure  S23 ). The global ST dataset is first decomposed into spatially contiguous patches based on coordinates, with the original spot indices preserved to maintain data integrity. Q    denotes the number of independent attention heads, where     W  1  q     denotes the trainable weight matrices for each head    q   .     a  t   t   i  j   q      refers to the normalized attention coefficients that quantify the interaction between spots    i    and    j   , computed via the attention weight vectors     a  q    . Non‐linear transformations are governed by activation functions     σ  1     and     σ  2    , which ensure the model captures complex spatial dependencies.  We encode spatial structural information using both the original spatial adjacency matrix     A  spatial     and the pruned adjacency matrix     A  pruned    . Propagating the first‐layer representation     H  1     through graph convolution under each adjacency yields two intermediate feature matrices,     H  spatial  1     and     H  pruned  1    . These representations are subsequently concatenated and projected by the second layer:
 
 (8)

 where     W  2     is a learnable weight matrix. The vector     h  i  2     is the embedding of spot    i   .  The decoder mirrors the encoder architecture and reconstructs the wavelet coefficient representation. Taking     H  2     as input, it first applies a graph attention–based aggregation to propagate neighborhood information, followed by a linear projection that maps the features back to wavelet coefficient space:

 (10)

 where     W  3     and     W  4     are trainable parameters.     H  3     and     H  4     are the corresponding layer outputs. The final reconstruction is      C  ^   =   H  4   ∈   R   n  ×   d  wc       . This design couples attention‐driven neighborhood aggregation with linear projection to achieve graph‐informed reconstruction.    4.7  Inverse Wavelet Transform  To more accurately recover spot‐level gene expression patterns, we apply the inverse discrete wavelet transform (IDWT) to both the reconstructed coefficient matrix     C  ^     and masked coefficient matrix     C  mask    . Specifically, we reverse the concatenation defined in Equations ( 3 ) and ( 4 ) to recover scale‐specific wavelet components. For each spot    i    (    i  =  1  ,  …  ,  n    ), a split operator maps the reconstructed coefficient vector      c  ^   i     to the set     (   a  J   ,   d  J   ,  …  ,   d  1   )    , where    J    denotes the number of wavelet decomposition levels.  We then perform the IDWT to recover the signal. The single‐level reconstruction is
 
 (11) 
        a   J  −  1     [  r  ]       =   ∑   k  =  0    N  −  1     h  ∼    [   r  −  2  k   ]     a  J    [  k  ]    +    ∑   k  =  0    N  −  1     g  ∼    [   r  −  2  k   ]     d  J    [  k  ]   ,       
 where     a  J     and     d  J     denote the approximation and detail coefficients at decomposition level    J   , respectively;     h  ∼     and     g  ∼     are the reconstruction low‐pass and high‐pass filters;    N    is the signal length at the current level; and    r    indexes the reconstructed samples. Iteratively applying Equation ( 11 ) from level    J    down to level     1     yields the reconstructed gene expression vector       x  ^   i   ∈   R  m      for spot    i   .  Stacking the reconstructed vectors      x  ^   i     across all spots yields the reconstructed expression matrix       X  ^   wc   ∈   R   n  ×  m      . Applying the same inverse discrete wavelet transform to the masked coefficient matrix     C  mask     produces      X  ^   mask    , which preserves low‐frequency approximation components while suppressing high‐frequency noise. Together, the pair     (    X  ^   wc   ,    X  ^   mask   )     provides complementary reconstructions that support robust downstream analysis.    4.8  Attention Fusion Mechanism  We integrate      X  ^   wc     and      X  ^   mask     using an attention‐based fusion module. The reconstruction      X  ^   wc     retains high‐frequency details but exhibits attenuated low‐frequency structure, while      X  ^   mask     preserves global low‐frequency trends while discarding fine‐scale variations. To balance these complementary properties, we employ spot‐level or gene‐level attention to adaptively weight the two reconstructions, yielding a more accurate and biologically faithful expression profile. Formally,
 
 (12) 
       γ  m      =    exp     a  m  ⊤    [     X  ^   wc   ∥    X  ^   mask    ]       ∑   j  =  1   2   exp     a  j  ⊤    [     X  ^   wc   ∥    X  ^   mask    ]      ,   m  ∈   {  1  ,  2  }   ,       
 
 
 (13)

 where     γ  m     denotes the learned attention coefficient, and the vectors     a  m     are trainable parameters, while    ⊙    represents element‐wise multiplication. This fusion mechanism enables complementary integration of low‐frequency structural information and high‐frequency detailed signals.    4.9  Loss Function  The objective function of STWave is formulated as a dual‐term loss that jointly optimizes reconstruction fidelity in both the wavelet and gene‐expression domains. The first term measures the reconstruction error of wavelet coefficients, preserving essential multiscale structural features, while the second term enforces accurate recovery of gene expression in the original space. The overall loss    L    is defined as
 
 (14) 
    min  L  =  α   1  n    ∑   i  =  1   n    ∥    C  i   −    C  ^   i    ∥  +    1  n    ∑   i  =  1   n    ∥   X  i   −    X  ^   i   ∥   ,    
 where     C  i     and      C  ^   i     denote the original and reconstructed wavelet representations for spot    i   , respectively;     X  i     and      X  ^   i     are the corresponding original and reconstructed gene expression vectors;    n    is the total number of spots; and    α    is a tunable hyperparameter controlling the contribution of the wavelet‐domain reconstruction term.    4.10  Training and Inference  After partitioning the original tissue slice into spatial patches, we randomize the patch order and train the model iteratively on each patch. As described above, the spot‐level expression vector is treated as a 1D discrete signal and transformed via a 1D discrete wavelet transform to obtain multiscale coefficients. These coefficients are processed by the autoencoder to generate reconstructed wavelet representations. The inverse discrete wavelet transform is then applied to map the reconstructed coefficients back to gene expression space, yielding a patch‐level reconstructed profile. In parallel, detail coefficients are masked and passed through the same inverse transform to produce a complementary reconstruction emphasizing low‐frequency structure. An attention‐based fusion module adaptively integrates the two reconstructions. Model training is guided by the loss function in Equation ( 14 ) and proceeds for a predefined number of epochs.  After training, inference is performed at the patch level to minimize GPU and CPU memory usage. Using the stored spot index sets, patch‐wise predictions are mapped back to their original spatial coordinates on the full tissue slice. This design substantially reduces computational overhead while preserving reconstruction fidelity (Figure  2a  and Figure  S1 ). The reconstructed expression profiles, together with the learned graph‐informed embeddings, are subsequently used for downstream tasks such as clustering, visualization, and spatial analysis.    4.11  Spatial Clustering  Following the above procedure, each spot is represented by a graph‐informed embedding and a reconstructed gene expression profile. We use the learned embeddings for spatial domain identification with standard clustering algorithms, including Mclust [ 48 ], Louvain [ 9 ], and Leiden [ 41 ]. For tissue slices with manual annotations, we apply Mclust and set the number of clusters to match the annotated domains. When annotations are unavailable or when latent spatial structure is to be discovered, we employ Louvain or Leiden clustering with an appropriately selected resolution. To ensure fair evaluation on annotated benchmarks, we follow the recommended settings for each method and tune the resolution parameters such that the inferred number of domains equals the annotation count, enabling balanced comparisons across methods.    4.12  Parameter Sensitivity Analysis  To evaluate the impact of the dual‐domain reconstruction loss weight    α    (defined in Equation ( 14 )) on model performance, we conducted a sensitivity analysis on the     12     human DLPFC slices. We varied the hyperparameter    α    from     5     to     30     in increments of     5     to assess its impact on clustering performance. As summarized in Tables  S10  and  S11 , STWave exhibits a clear performance trend, achieving optimal results at     α  =  20    . At this setting, the model attains the highest clustering accuracy, with a mean ARI of     0.642     and a mean NMI of     0.654    .  Further analysis of mean and variance across different    α    underscores the robustness of STWave. Although performance peaks at     α  =  20    , clustering accuracy remains stable throughout the evaluated range, indicating limited sensitivity to moderate hyperparameter variations. Notably, at     α  =  20    , the standard deviation of NMI is minimized (    0.045    ), while the standard deviation of ARI remains low (    0.089    ). This consistently low variance across 12 tissue slices suggests that a fixed setting of     α  =  20     generalizes well across samples without requiring slice‐specific tuning. To further assess whether this setting transfers beyond DLPFC, the same sensitivity analysis was performed on the Xenium human breast cancer dataset and the mouse embryo dataset using three independent random seeds. On the Xenium dataset,     α  =  20     achieved the highest ARI (    0.441  ±  0.026    ) and a comparable NMI (    0.549  ±  0.001    ) across the tested range. On the mouse embryo dataset,     α  =  20     achieved the highest ARI (    0.415  ±  0.018    ) and NMI (    0.612  ±  0.001    ) (Tables  S12  and  S13 ). These results demonstrate that STWave exhibits a stable optimization landscape and strong generalization performance.     Conflicts of Interest  The authors declare no conflicts of interest. evidence_text:
DeSpaST: deconvoluting spatial transcriptomics signals to cell-level resolution using histology images. Advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies enable spatially resolved gene expression profiling, yet most platforms remain limited to spot-level resolution, where each measurement aggregates signals from multiple cells and obscures cell-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Existing computational approaches either provide limited sub-spot refinement or rely on matched single-cell RNA sequencing references that are costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we present DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network that deconvolves spot-level ST data into cell-level gene expression profiles using only paired histology images. DeSpaST extracts nucleus-level morphological features, constructs directed cellular interaction graphs, and integrates spatial and transcriptional information through message passing. Validated across four cancer datasets with orthogonal Xenium, immunofluorescence, ablation, and interslice evaluations, DeSpaST enhances spatial resolution, facilitates downstream cellular-level analyses, and provides deeper insights into tissue biology. Background  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have made significant progress in transitioning transcriptomic research from the cell level to a 2D spatial cell system. This transition is crucial for investigating cell–cell communication, tissue heterogeneity, and the tumor microenvironment, offering new insights into intricate biological processes. In contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which requires tissue dissociation, ST technologies profile gene expression and preserve the spatial composition of cells within the native tissue environment [ 1 ]. ST technologies (e.g. 10× Genomics Visium [ 2 ], Nanostring GeoMx DSP [ 3 ], HDST [ 4 ], and Slide-seq [ 5 ]) utilize unique spatial barcodes to label the spatial locations and capture the gene expression at thousands of barcoded spatial locations (referred to as spots) within one experiment [ 6 ]. While these methods achieve high detection efficiency, their spatial resolution is inherently limited. The barcoded spot area (Spot diameter: 10× Genomics Visium: 55 μm, Nanostring GeoMx DSP: 10 μm [ 7 ], and Slide-seq: 10 μm [ 8 ]) encompasses a diverse population of cells, ranging from a few cells up to 200 cells [ 9 ]. To accurately distinguish the mixed-cell populations and uncover biological inferences from the ST data, it is essential to develop computational models that can enhance the resolution of ST data.  Several computational methods have been developed to improve the spatial resolution of ST data. Bayesian-based methods such as BayesSpace [ 10 ] refine gene expression to sub-spot resolution, only yielding modest improvement. Deep-learning-based approaches such as SPOTlight [ 11 ], Tangram [ 12 ], cell2location [ 13 ], and CARD [ 14 ] integrate ST data with scRNA-seq data, mapping related gene expression cells to ST coordinates or reconstructing the ST landscape from various cell combinations. However, the reliance on scRNA-seq data significantly raises the experimental costs and introduces constraints, including limited cell types and potential biases in spatial reconstruction accuracy.  Instead of relying on the scRNA-seq data, integrating histology images with ST data presents a more feasible and promising way to enhance ST resolution. Most ST platforms, such as Visium and HDST, typically provide corresponding histology images, like hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining images, which offer high-resolution morphological and spatial information for individual cells across the tissue sections. Deep-learning-based methods such as TESLA [ 15 ], XFuse [ 16 ], and iStar [ 17 ] have been developed to integrate the histology image with ST data to enhance ST resolution. However, these methods primarily enhance resolution at the pixel level but fall short of achieving cell-level gene expression resolution. Furthermore, these methods focus on extracting pixel level histological features [e.g. pixel intensities in red, green, blue (RGB) channels], neglecting true cell features and cell–cell interactions, which compromises model accuracy. A specialized model that directly incorporates actual cell-level features is necessary to improve the biological application of ST data.  Many fundamental biological questions—including the delineation of cell-type boundaries, characterization of the tumor microenvironment, and inference of cell–cell communication—inherently require cell-level resolution. However, true single-cell spatial assays such as Xenium or MERFISH remain expensive, limited in gene panel size, and not universally available, making spot-level ST the dominant modality in practice. Moreover, matched scRNA-seq data from the same tissue, which several existing deconvolution methods depend on, is not always obtainable and may introduce additional biases when tissue dissociation alters cell-type composition. A computational approach that can reliably infer cell-level expression directly from spot-level ST data and routine histology images therefore addresses a practical and widely encountered gap in the field.  In this work, we developed an innovative model called DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), which incorporates the cell level features from histology image with ST data using dynamic edge–conditioned graph convolution neural network ( Fig. 1 , and  Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Starting with a histology image, we perform cell segmentation and explicitly extract cell morphological and spatial interaction features, followed by constructing the cellular graphic interaction structures of the tissue. We then build a graph deconvolution model that combines ST data with these morphological features and interaction structures to deconvolute spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression profiles. In contrast to the previous methods that primarily rely on pixel-level information and use convolutional neural network (CNN)-like structures to encode the features, which often failing to capture cell–cell interaction information. DeSpaST leverages the graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fully capture the cellular interaction topologies by constructing cellular interaction graphic structures. Unlike conventional CNNs, GCNs operate on non-Euclidean data structures, enabling comprehensive modeling of diverse cellular interaction topologies. DeSpaST offers several practical advantages. First, it does not require scRNA-seq references, reducing experimental cost and avoiding dependence on matched dissociated-cell datasets. Second, it leverages morphology and local tissue architecture to improve spatial localization and denoising within spots, which is particularly valuable in heterogeneous tumors where boundaries and niches vary over short distances. Third, DeSpaST’s inferred cell-level expression supports downstream analyses that are difficult at spot resolution, such as cell-type mapping at cellular granularity, spatial domain characterization, and trajectory inference. In our experiments, these advantages manifest as improved agreement with orthogonal measurements (e.g. Xenium), clearer spatial patterns, and improved recovery of spatial domains, with robustness supported by ablations demonstrating that performance depends on both transcriptional input and morphology rather than visual cues alone. Together, these considerations motivate DeSpaST as a practical and interpretable approach for cell-level resolution inference from spot-based ST, while clarifying the conditions under which it is most reliable.    Result   Overview of the DeSpaST model  DeSpaST requires only two inputs: a histology image and ST data ( Fig. 1a ). Histology images offer the individual cell spatial organization and morphology characterization, while the ST data provide gene expression at the spot level. To explicitly extract the cell spatial and organization characterizations from the histology image, we first employed the HD-staining deep-learning algorithm [ 18 ,  19 ] to segment and classify the cell nucleus from the tissue image. Alternatively, other methods for cell or nuclei segmentation could also be applied at this step. We then extracted the morphology features for each cell to construct the cellular graphic structures (see  Fig. 1a  and  Method  section for details). DeSpaST builds the graphic convolution networks by performing the four following steps: (i) extract image patches based on the spot coordinates in the ST data; (ii) construct a directed cellular graphic structure for each patch using nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance from a cell to its neighbors; and (iii) derive features from the directed cellular graphic structures to incorporate the spatial and morphology information of the cells into the graph convolutional network. Each node in the graph represents a cell. Node features include cell size, shape, and other morphological features. Edges denote spatial and morphological relationships between cells. Edge features include cell spatial proximity, cell connectivity angle, and interaction edge categorization ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) [ 4 ]. The model is then constructed using two convolutional layers and one fully connected layer ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). All cell nodes are updated through a message passing from all neighboring nodes in each convolutional layer, which incorporates both morphological and cell–cell spatial interaction features of neighboring cells. In this study, we demonstrate DeSpaST’s ability in accurately capturing cell-level gene expression to overcoming spatial resolution limitations in ST data, using breast, lung, and ovarian cancer datasets as examples. DeSpaST offers a new convenient tool for advancing biomedical research, with broad applicability to diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets.    DeSpaST effectively enhances gene expression resolution  To assess the efficacy of DeSpaST, we applied the model to a well-studied breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. We then conducted a comparative analysis of DeSpaST’s performance against the TESLA model [ 15 ], which is a machine-learning framework designed to enhance gene expression to pixel-level resolution [ 15 ]. DeSpaST demonstrated notable advancements in elucidating gene expression patterns. To illustrate, we present two marker genes,  MS4A1  and  ERBB2 , as representative examples ( Fig. 1b ). The  MS4A1  gene encodes the surface molecule CD20, which serves as a widely recognized marker indicative of B-cell lineage [ 21 ].  ERBB2  encodes the human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2) protein [ 22 ], which is used as a tumor marker in breast cancer diagnosis [ 23 ,  24 ]. For each gene, the cell-level gene expression profile from DeSpaST, spot-level gene expression pattern from Visium ST data, and the pixel-level gene expression patterns from TESLA ( Fig. 1b ), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ) were plotted separately. Compared to Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse, DeSpaST showed the gene expression profiles with highest clarity and precision for both genes, successfully enhancing the gene expression resolution. Notably, the gene expression patterns from DeSpaST correlated well with the pathologist-annotated regions. DeSpaST high  ERBB2  gene expression cells closely matched the pathologist-annotated tumor regions. Also, the DeSpaST high  MS4A1  expressed cells were well aligned with the annotated immune cell regions. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse did not achieve the same level of visual clarity as DeSpaST in these regions. The  MS4A1  gene expression profile is particularly noteworthy because it is nearly imperceptible in the Visium ST data and in the reconstructions produced by TESLA ( Fig. 1b , right), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3b ), whereas DeSpaST accurately discerns the  MS4A1  gene expression pattern and immune cell regions.  Remarkably, DeSpaST’s cell-level gene expression predictions demonstrate its capability and reliability in distinguishing between different cell layers. In three specific areas ( Fig. 1c  and  d , and  Supplementary Fig. S4 ), pathologists meticulously annotated the invasive carcinoma and immune cell regions to delineate their boundaries in the H&E images. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST effectively differentiated between these immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST accurately captured the elevated expression of ERBB2 in tumor regions and the elevated expression of MS4A1 in immune cell regions. The distinct gene expression patterns of MS4A1 and ERBB2 predicted by DeSpaST ( Fig. 1c  and  d  ,  and  Supplementary Fig. S4b ) precisely delineated the tumor and immune boundaries. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse could not accurately delineate these cell layers and boundaries ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ); instead, they only provided ambiguous patterns, which indicates a lack of precision in defining the regions. Moreover, as shown in  Supplementary Fig. S4c , DeSpaST demonstrated exceptional potential in precise cell type annotation. Beyond the highly expressed ERBB2 tumor region, DeSpaST identified an additional layer outside the tumor region with abundant MS4A1 expression, which had not been previously annotated. Upon closer examination of the H&E image by the pathologist, the layer was found to be a lightly stained layer, containing fibrous connective tissues interspersed with inflammatory cells, crucial for restricting tumor expansion. This finding of interspersed immune cells is consistent with the MS4A1 gene expression pattern predicted by DeSpaST.    DeSpaST accurately predicts cellular-level gene expression  The above comparison between pathology annotation and DeSpaST highlights the resolution enhancement power of DeSpaST. To further evaluate the model’s performance, we conducted a direct and comprehensive comparison of cellular-level expression for individual genes. In addition to the Visium spot-level gene expression measurement, Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] also measured the cellular-level gene expression of hundreds of genes through the Xenium experiment. We applied DeSpaST to this breast cancer Visium dataset from Janesick  et al . [ 25 ], segmented and classified the cell nucleus from the H&E image ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), and deconvolving spot-level ST signals into cell-level gene expression profiles. Despite the inherent limitations of adjacent-section comparisons (e.g. local distortion, cell displacement, and microenvironmental differences), DeSpaST showed strong concordance with Xenium in spatial distribution patterns. For example, for the breast cancer marker gene  CCND1  [ 26 ,  27 ] ( Fig. 2a ) and T-cell marker gene  CD69  [ 28 ,  29 ] ( Fig. 2b ), DeSpaST accurately predicted the gene expression patterns, in agreement with the observed patterns in the Xenium. Both Visium and TESLA failed to resolve these patterns adequately, especially in the complex tissue regions. Consider the top of the tissue section ( Fig. 2c  and  Supplementary Fig. S6a ) where intricate tumor and immune cell domains are present. Only DeSpaST successfully captured gene expression within intricate microenvironments ( Fig. 2d  and  e ), accurately reflecting the patterns observed in the Xenium experiment. Conversely, TESLA and Visium failed to capture these spatial variations in gene expression, resulting in unclear expression patterns. In the case of the  CD69  gene ( Fig. 2b ), the Visium ST data are noisy and lack a clear expression pattern. Although TESLA reduces some noise, it fails to capture the inherent gene expression patterns accurately. In contrast, DeSpaST effectively eliminates noise and accurately discerns the true gene expression pattern.    Figure 2   Evaluation of DeSpaST in cell-level gene expression prediction. With the gene pattern identified by DeSpaST, our next step involves a quantitative assessment of the performance enhancement achieved by the DeSpaST model. To facilitate this assessment, spot-level gene expression was reconstructed by taking the average expression of cells inside each spot. For quantitative comparison across methods, we reconstructed spot-level expression by averaging the predicted cellular expressions within each Visium spot and then computed gene-wise Pearson correlations against Xenium for DeSpaST, raw Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DeSpaST exhibits a stronger correlation to Xenium ( r  = 0.754 for  CCND1  gene and  r  = 0.665 for  CD69  gene) than both Visium ( r  = 0.477 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.239 for  CD69  gene) and TESLA ( r  = 0.720 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.424 for  CD69  gene) ( Fig. 2f  and  Supplementary Fig. S3c ). Similar enhancements in clarity and noise reduction in gene expression patterns were observed in other genes as well, such as the  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  genes ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ). DeSpaST demonstrated strong consistency with Xenium experiments for both of these genes, achieving a correlation of  r  = 0.850 for the  ERBB2  gene and  r  = 0.610 for the  MS4A1  gene ( Supplementary Fig. S7c  and  d ). In addition to the above genes, to assess transcriptome-wide generalizability, we computed spot-level Pearson correlations for all examined Xenium genes and summarize the overall trend using correlation density plots ( Fig. 2g ;  Supplementary Fig. S3c ): DeSpaST achieves higher overall agreement with Xenium (median  r  = 0.518) than Visium (median  r  = 0.198) and TESLA (median  r  = 0.479), and the top 20% highest-density region summary consistently favors DeSpaST, indicating systematic improvement beyond a small set of marker genes.  To address the concern that histology-guided models might rely on visual cues and to validate key graph-construction hyperparameters, we performed a comprehensive set of ablation and sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). First, randomizing the input transcriptional counts (“Random count”) caused a substantial collapse in performance—gene-wise correlation with Xenium dropped (CD69:  r  = 0.188; CCND1:  r  = 0.379), the overall summary decreased (top 20% high-density mean correlation: 0.174), and downstream spatial domain agreement deteriorated (NMI: 0.033; ARI: 0.0196)—demonstrating that accurate transcriptional signals are essential and that morphology alone cannot recover meaningful spatial expression. Second, randomizing morphology features (“Random image info”) also reduced performance relative to the full model (e.g. CD69:  r  = 0.423 versus 0.665; top 20% high-density mean: 0.202 versus 0.582; NMI: 0.169 versus 0.194; ARI: 0.0910 versus 0.1167), indicating that morphology provides complementary information but is not solely responsible for DeSpaST’s gains. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of the k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) cell-graph parameter by varying        on the breast dataset: extreme values were suboptimal (e.g. top-20%-density mean correlation = 0.161 at        and 0.220 at       ), while intermediate values (      –12) consistently achieved higher performance (0.58–0.64) and stable domain-detection agreement, supporting our choice of        as a balance between locality and connectivity ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Together, these analyses show that DeSpaST integrates both transcriptional and morphological information and that its performance is stable across a biologically reasonable range of neighborhood sizes.  To further test whether the deconvoluted outputs preserve biologically meaningful spatial structure beyond individual marker genes, we evaluated each method using a downstream spatial domain detection task on the breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. As shown in ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), we used the manually annotated domains as ground-truth labels. For each tool, we took the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as input, constructed (i) an expression kNN graph in PCA space and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in 2D coordinate space, fused them into a hybrid connectivity matrix, and inferred domains using Leiden community detection (parameters reported in Supplementary Information). We then quantified concordance with manual annotations using NMI and ARI ( Supplementary Fig. S9b ; higher is better). DeSpaST achieved the best agreement with manual labels (NMI = 0.194; ARI = 0.117), outperforming iStar (NMI = 0.182; ARI = 0.056), XFuse (NMI = 0.033; ARI = 0.011), and TESLA (NMI = 0.143; ARI = 0.031), indicating that DeSpaST’s deconvolution better preserves domain-level organization for downstream spatial analyses.  Supplementary Fig. S9c  further visualizes the inferred domains from each method, where DeSpaST produces domain boundaries that are qualitatively more consistent with the expert annotations.  The remarkable cell-level resolution achieved by DeSpaST creates new possibilities for examining cell–cell communications within a spatial context. For instance, within the cellular milieu surrounding the breast ducts ( Supplementary Fig. S10 ), we detected elevated expressions of breast cancer marker genes  CCND1  and  ERBB2  ( Supplementary Fig. S10a  and  c ). In contrast, immune cell marker genes  CD69  and  MS4A1  ( Supplementary Fig. S10b  and  d ) exhibited high expression in the outside layer adjacent to the tumor cells. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST align with the Xenium gene panel, while TESLA failed to predict them accurately. DeSpaST’s findings suggest possible interactions between immune and tumor cells, highlighting its potential for further studies on the tissue microenvironment and cell–cell communication. Next, we evaluate whether the gene expression patterns obtained by DeSpaST could reflect protein expressions at the cell level [ 25 ]. We plotted and compared the  MS4A1  and  ERBB2  gene expression patterns with the corresponding HER2 and CD20 protein immunofluorescence (IF) signals ( Fig. 3a  and  b ). Interestingly, the gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST closely align with protein expression profiles, while Visium and TESLA are not able to capture them. We calculated the correlations between predicted  MS4A1  gene expression and Xenium IF CD20 protein signals. DeSpaST exhibits superior performance compared to TESLA and Visium with higher correlation ( r  = 0.622 for DeSpaST versus  r  = 0.420 for Visium and  r  = 0.401 for TESLA;  Fig. 3c ). DeSpaST also demonstrated a notably higher correlation of ERBB2 gene expression with HER2 protein expression ( r  = 0.839) when compared to Visium ( r  = 0.821) and TESLA ( r  = 0.660), as illustrated in  Fig. 3d . Although Visium and TESLA also showed good correlations with the HER2 IF signals, DeSpaST significantly outperformed them in predicting fine-grained details gene expression patterns ( Supplementary Fig. S11 ). Notably, only DeSpaST accurately captured the comprehensive pattern of ERBB2 gene expression, depicting the tumor’s shape around the breast duct in alignment with IF protein signals. In contrast, Visium and TESLA predicted a vague outline of ERBB2 expression, lacking finer details and failing to depict a clear pattern. Application of DeSpaST for cell type identification  Given the highly precise cell-level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST, we employed DeSpaST for downstream analysis. This involved leveraging the predicted cell-level gene expression to delineate the spatial distribution of various cell types. Unlike ST data, where one spot may contain multiple cells, DeSpaST’s cellular-level resolution offers a superior depiction of cell-type distribution. Utilizing DeSpaST’s gene expression predictions as input, we applied the cell-type identification algorithm ScType [ 32 ] to assign the cell type to each single cell. The resulting cell-type profiles were mapped back onto the spatial location and detected locations for tumor cells, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages ( Supplementary Fig. S12a ). To validate the cell-type distribution by DeSpaST, we implemented the ScType algorithm with the Xenium data and plotted the cell-type distribution in  Supplementary Fig. S12b . The spatial distributions of annotated cell types from DeSpaST closely resemble the cell types obtained from Xenium, which further substantiate the accuracy of DeSpaST. To reveal the tumor’s immunological response, we specifically focus on tumor cells and immune cells ( Fig. 4a  and  b ). Both DeSpaST ( Fig. 4a ) and Xenium panel ( Fig. 4b ) delineated similar tumor and immune cell regions. Heterogeneous areas are found at the upper and middle portion of the tissue where tumor and immune cells closely interact, which indicates the recognition and attack of activated immune cells that impede tumor spread. In contrast, tumor regions at the lower portion of the slides appear less confined, forming dense and more aggressive tumor areas where there is a lack of immune cell control. Both Xenium and DeSpaST accurately classify these complex cell environments. While Xenium served as a valuable reference here, DeSpaST exhibits greater potential and offers the flexibility to include more marker genes for cell type classification analysis. Unlike Xenium's panel of 306 genes, DeSpaST can leverage the transcriptomic level gene expression data from ST data. This enables the inclusion of a wider range of cell-type markers, leading to more accurate classification.    Figure 4   Application of DeSpaST in spatial cell-level downstream analysis. Application of DeSpaST in uncovering pseudo temporal trajectories of tumor progression  Following the annotation of cancer cells, we calculated the pseudo-trajectories timeline of tumor development based on the inferred cell level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST. The partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) method was used to construct the topological graph and a cluster with high expression of cancer stem cell marker  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ] was selected as the root node ( Supplementary Fig. S13 ). Pseudotime values were estimated and mapped back to each cell's spatial location to infer the dynamic trajectories of tumor progression ( Fig. 4c ). Interestingly, the clusters of early pseudotime cancer cells and late pseudotime cancer cells occupy markedly distinct regions in the tissue section. These distributions align precisely with the DCIS (ductal carcinoma  in situ ) and invasive tumor regions annotated by expert pathologists ( Fig. 4d ). Tumor cells with early pseudotime exhibit a denser and more uniform composition characterized with reduced variability in size and shape, corresponding to DCIS regions ( Fig. 4d ). In contrast, late pseudotime tumor cells, located in the invasive tumor region, show increased invasivenexss and a more loosely organized structure. Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships.    Auto graph convolutional network for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution  Following the construction of the cellular graphic structure and thoughtfully derived essential node and edge features, we employed dynamic edge-conditioned convolution to manage graphs of varying size and connectivity. This process is mathematically represented in Equation ( 1 ). The embedding vector of the convolution filter is then used to deconvolve the spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression. Our model-specific architecture comprises of three layers: two ECC (Edge-Conditioned Convolution) [ 50 ,  51 ] GCN layers [ 52 ,  53 ] followed by a ReLU activation function [ 54 ], and one linear transformation layer. Each ECC layer incorporates both node and edge feature embeddings for propagating information across the graph ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. To achieve a precise and efficient registration, we systematically tested various combinations of angles and scales between the IF and H&E images. To optimize computing efficiency, we initially conducted tests with 10% scaled-down images to obtain approximate scale and angle adjustments. Subsequently, we fine-tuned the registration using the original scale.    DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts. title: Geranium: Multimodal Retrieval of Genomics Data Visualizations.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Geranium: Multimodal Retrieval of Genomics Data Visualizations. Effective visualization is essential for interpreting genomics data, yet researchers often face challenges in finding relevant, reusable examples. Existing tools offer limited support for searching the vast landscape of genomics visualizations, making the process of authoring new visualizations time-consuming and inefficient. To address this gap, we introduce Geranium, a data visualization retrieval system for searching and authoring genomics visualizations. Geranium supports multimodal retrieval, enabling users to query with images, text, or grammar-based specifications. Retrieved examples serve as scaffolds for authoring, providing templates that researchers can adapt with their own data, thereby streamlining the mechanics of visualization construction. Geranium integrates three embedding methods to combine specialized and general knowledge: grammar-based embeddings tailored to genomics visualizations, multimodal embeddings from a biomedical vision-language foundation model, and text embeddings from a fine-tuned large language model. For each visualization, we construct a multimodal representation that includes a Gosling specification, a pixel-based rendering, and natural language descriptions. We evaluate embedding strategies to maximize top-$k$k retrieval accuracy and conduct user studies with domain collaborators to gather feedback on usability. Our collection comprises 3,200 visualizations across 50 categories, ranging from single-view to coordinated multi-view designs and supporting applications from single-cell epigenomics to structural variation analysis.

title: Deep Learning Image Processing Models in Dermatopathology.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Deep Learning Image Processing Models in Dermatopathology. Dermatopathology has rapidly advanced due to the implementation of deep learning models and artificial intelligence (AI). From convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformer-based foundation models, these systems are now capable of accurate whole-slide analysis and multimodal integration. This review synthesizes the most recent advents of deep-learning architecture and synthesizes its evolution from first-generation CNNs to hybrid CNN-transformer systems to large-scale foundational models such as Paige's PanDerm AI and Virchow. Herein, we examine performance benchmarks from real-world deployments of major dermatopathology deep learning models (DermAI, PathAssist Derm), as well as emerging next-generation models still under research and development. We assess barriers to clinical workflow adoption such as dataset bias, AI interpretability, and government regulation. Further, we discuss potential future research directions and emphasize the need for diverse, prospectively curated datasets, explainability frameworks for trust in AI, and rigorous compliance to Good Machine-Learning-Practice (GMLP) to achieve safe and scalable deep learning dermatopathology models that can fully integrate into clinical workflows.

title: A Unified Information Bottleneck Framework for Multimodal Biomedical Machine Learning.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: A Unified Information Bottleneck Framework for Multimodal Biomedical Machine Learning. Multimodal biomedical machine learning increasingly integrates heterogeneous data sources (including medical imaging, multi-omics profiles, electronic health records, and wearable sensor signals) to support clinical diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response prediction. Despite strong empirical performance, most existing multimodal systems lack a principled theoretical foundation for understanding why fusion improves prediction, how information is distributed across modalities, and when models can be trusted under incomplete or shifting data. This paper develops a unified information-theoretic framework that formalizes multimodal biomedical learning as an information optimization problem. We formulate multimodal representation learning through the information bottleneck principle, deriving a variational objective that balances predictive sufficiency against informational compression in an architecture-agnostic manner. Building on this foundation, we introduce information-theoretic tools for decomposing modality contributions via conditional mutual information, quantifying redundancy and synergy, and diagnosing fusion collapse. We further show that robustness to missing modalities can be cast as an information consistency problem and extend the framework to longitudinal disease modeling through transfer entropy and sequential information bottleneck objectives. Applications to multimodal foundation models, uncertainty quantification, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection are developed. Empirical case studies across three biomedical datasets (TCGA breast cancer multi-omics, TCGA glioma clinical-plus-molecular data, and OASIS-2 longitudinal Alzheimer's data) show that the framework's key quantities are computable and interpretable on real data: MI decomposition identifies modality dominance and redundancy; the VMIB traces a compression-prediction tradeoff in the information plane; entropy-based selective prediction raises accuracy from 0.787 to 0.939 at 50% coverage; transfer entropy reveals stage-dependent modality influence in disease progression; and pretraining/adaptation diagnostics distinguish efficient from wasteful fine-tuning strategies. Together, these results develop entropy and mutual information as organizing principles for the design, analysis, and evaluation of multimodal biomedical AI systems.

title: PhenoModel: A multimodal phenotypic drug design foundation model for discovering novel potential inhibitors of multiple cancer cells.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: PhenoModel: A multimodal phenotypic drug design foundation model for discovering novel potential inhibitors of multiple cancer cells. Phenotypic drug discovery (PDD) focuses on the observable traits or phenotype of cells or organisms in response to drug treatment, rather than relying primarily on specific molecular targets. Drugs discovered through this approach may have better therapeutic relevance, as they are tested in conditions that closely mimic human disease. In this study, we present PhenoModel, a multimodal molecular foundation model developed using our unique dual-space contrastive learning framework. This model effectively connects molecular structures with phenotypic information. PhenoModel is applicable to a range of downstream drug discovery tasks, including molecular property prediction and active molecule screening based on targets, phenotypes, and ligands. Our results demonstrate that PhenoModel outperforms baseline methods in these areas. Building from this model, PhenoScreen is developed to successfully identify several phenotypically bioactive compounds against osteosarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines. These findings highlight the versatility of PhenoModel and its potential to accelerate drug discovery by uncovering novel therapeutic pathways and expanding the diversity of viable drug candidates.

title: General artificial intelligence for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer: the rise of foundation models.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: General artificial intelligence for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer: the rise of foundation models. Artificial intelligence (AI) and its computer algorithms, including those of machine learning and deep learning, have been transforming the oncology field. Generative AI (Gen AI) and general AI technologies, which can be adapted to various tasks based on diverse inputs, are being increasingly utilized in healthcare applications. Foundation models, driven by Gen AI and general AI technologies, have enthralled the medical world, representing the next generation of large-scale AI tools in medicine that are trained on massive amounts of data and will make a major impact due to their versatility, high performance, personalization enhancement, and assistance of healthcare workers. That said, it is undeniable that there are multiple obstacles that these algorithms must overcome to be successfully utilized in the field. In this review, we first present a brief background and a history of the recent rise of Gen AI and foundation models. Next, we explore their applications in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, specifically in radiology, pathology, precision medicine, personalization of care, and surgical oncology. Then, we discuss some of the limitations that could hinder general and Gen AI's clinical translation.

title: Impact of tissue staining and scanner variation on the performance of pathology foundation models: a study of sarcomas and their mimics
